item.title: Alerts Are Not Suspicion: How Crypto AML Turns Risk Signals into Actionable Intelligence
item.dc:creator: SlowMist
item.content:encoded:
In day-to-day anti-money laundering (AML) operations, on-chain risk alerts, address labels, and risk scores have become important tools for identifying suspicious leads. However, once an alert is triggered, the real challenges are only beginning.

Recently, Basel Institute on Governance and The Wolfsberg Group released a discussion paper summarizing the outcomes of a session they organized during the Global Conference on Criminal Finances and Cryptoassets, held in Luxembourg on September 15, 2026. The paper focuses on an issue worthy of industry attention: how to turn risk signals identified through on-chain analysis into meaningful STR/SAR intelligence that can support subsequent investigations.

Original report: https://baselgovernance.org/cms/api/assets/8db165c2-0a7a-4da8-837c-ebef361a3780/Crypto-STR-report_final.pdf?v=20261111131910000

I. Alerts Are Not Conclusions in Themselves

Unusual activity and suspicious activity are not the same thing.

A system-generated alert indicates that certain behavior warrants attention, but the alert itself cannot replace an assessment of the surrounding context, nor can it automatically serve as sufficient grounds for filing an STR/SAR.

The report points out that institutions frequently face a conflict between timeliness and investigative completeness in practice:

If a report is filed too early, it may be based only on preliminary alerts and limited contextual information, without sufficient analysis. If too much time is spent investigating, institutions may face pressure from reporting deadlines, resource constraints, and internal processes. If information remains incomplete, institutions must also determine whether the available evidence is already sufficient to support reasonable suspicion.

This is particularly relevant in cases involving incomplete information and complex business models, where institutions need to exercise professional judgment and assess whether the applicable reporting thresholds under relevant legal and regulatory frameworks have been met based on the information available.

This also means that the role of risk monitoring systems is to help institutions identify activities warranting further investigation, not to replace compliance professionals in making final decisions.

II. The Key to a Valuable Report Is Clearly Explaining What Happened

The report summarizes the core elements of a high-quality STR/SAR as enabling the recipient to understand the relevant activity, the investigative steps taken by the institution, and how the suspicion was formed.

III. Beware of Defensive Reporting

Defensive reporting refers to situations in which institutions primarily file reports to avoid criticism or penalties, rather than based on genuine suspicion formed through sufficient analysis.

A large volume of reports that lack context, contain limited analysis, or simply reproduce tool outputs may create processing pressure for both reporting institutions and the competent authorities receiving the reports. It can also make it more difficult for Financial Intelligence Units (FIUs) to prioritize information.

When evaluating the value of reporting activities, attention should be paid to information quality, contextual completeness, and usefulness for subsequent investigations, rather than simply the number of reports submitted.

At the same time, the report does not attribute reporting quality issues solely to frontline analysts. Analysts’ experience, institutional control frameworks, compliance culture, data quality, regulatory expectations, and FIUs’ capacity to provide feedback all influence whether reports can be effectively prepared. For teams with limited resources, finding an appropriate balance between timeliness, investigative depth, and proportionality remains a practical challenge.

The report also notes that experienced analysts are generally better equipped to distinguish genuine suspicion from routine monitoring alerts. Automated systems can improve the efficiency of identifying leads, but they cannot replace contextual analysis of specific activities.

IV. On-Chain Analysis Should Go Beyond Risk Scores

Blockchain analytics tools can help institutions monitor fund flows, identify connections between addresses, and support network-level analysis. The report recognizes the value of these tools in cryptoasset-related investigations while also highlighting their limitations.

One important issue is entity attribution.

The association between blockchain addresses and real individuals, businesses, or services may be affected by data completeness, attribution methodologies, and analytical techniques. Different blockchain analytics service providers may use different data sources, clustering techniques, and analytical methodologies. As a result, they may sometimes reach different conclusions about the same activity.

This means that risk scores and address labels need to be understood in light of the analytical basis behind them, rather than treated as independent, automatic, and unquestionable conclusions.

The report suggests that more valuable analysis typically combines blockchain analytics with other sources of information, such as:

  • Customer Due Diligence (CDD) information;
  • Transaction monitoring results;
  • Internal account activity;
  • Customer behavioral indicators;
  • Open-Source Intelligence (OSINT).

Behavioral indicators may also provide important insights, including transaction timing, connections between bank accounts and customers, IP addresses, VPN usage, and links to Over-the-Counter (OTC) activities.

The report also raises the issue of explainability: the FIU receiving a report may not have access to the same analytics platforms, datasets, or entity attribution methodologies used by the reporting institution. If a report provides only a risk conclusion without explaining the analytical basis behind it, the recipient may find it difficult to understand how that conclusion was reached.

Where permitted under the applicable reporting framework, genuinely necessary, and consistent with the principle of proportionality, providing relevant excerpts of analytical results or explaining the basis of analytical outputs can help recipients understand the assessment.

V. Practical Challenges for Institutions: Leads, Information, and Resources Are Not Always Available

Beyond the limitations of analytical tools themselves, the report also discusses several challenges institutions face in conducting investigations in practice.

1. High Alert Volumes and Limited Investigative Resources

Institutions may face large volumes of transactions and risk alerts simultaneously. Teams must identify significant cases in a timely manner while avoiding the mechanical escalation of every alert into a formal report.

2. Risk Exposure Can Extend Beyond One Hop, and the Degree of Association Needs to Be Explained

Checking only deposit addresses may fail to reveal the upstream source of funds. Looking only at direct transactions may also overlook risks propagated through multiple intermediate addresses.

Conversely, reaching a high-risk conclusion simply because an address has had an indirect connection with a risky entity, without considering the associated amount, proportion of funds, and number of hops in the transaction path, may also lead to misjudgments.

3. On-Chain and Off-Chain Information Is Scattered Across Different Parties

Banks and payment institutions may have visibility into fiat fund flows and customer account behavior, while Crypto-Asset Service Providers (CASPs) may have access to internal platform data and some on-chain activity. Other participants may hold different pieces of information.

The report points out that no single institution necessarily has the complete picture. Within the limits permitted by law, confidentiality requirements, and operational conditions, cooperation between the public and private sectors, as well as communication among private-sector institutions, can help fill information gaps across different stages. In particular, information exchange between traditional financial institutions and CASPs may help both parties gain a more comprehensive understanding of customer activity.

4. Historical Fund Tracing Has Practical Limitations

One important issue discussed in the report, and one particularly relevant to institutions’ day-to-day operations, is how far back institutions should trace the historical activity of cryptoassets.

Customer funds may pass through multiple exchanges, self-hosted wallets, DeFi services, or different jurisdictions. Relevant platforms may have ceased operations, and historical records may be missing. Even when a customer’s explanation of the source of wealth is generally consistent, or the funds ultimately originate from a regulated service provider, this does not necessarily prove that every stage of the historical transaction path can be fully reconstructed.

VI. Practical Takeaways

Based on the discussions in the report, the key directions for improving the effectiveness of cryptoasset-related STR/SAR reporting can be summarized in the following eight points:

  1. Focus on intelligence value, not report volume. Reporting quality should not be measured by the number of submissions, but by whether reports provide competent authorities with valuable information that can support subsequent investigations.
  2. Treat alerts and risk signals as starting points for analysis, not direct grounds for filing reports. Risk scores, system alerts, and unusual transactions are investigative leads. Whether a report should be filed should still depend on the specific circumstances and professional judgment.
  3. Clearly explain the basis for forming suspicion. A high-quality report should describe the specific characteristics of the suspicious activity, the information reviewed, the investigative steps taken, and how the relevant evidence supports the final assessment.
  4. Ensure data accuracy and use structured, machine-readable formats. Complete and accurate information on individuals, entities, accounts, and transactions, together with structured data formats such as XML, can help FIUs link information across different reports, including cross-border information.
  5. Combine blockchain analytics with other information sources. Blockchain analytics tools should support, rather than replace, human judgment. Combining on-chain analysis with customer due diligence, transaction monitoring, behavioral indicators, and open-source intelligence can help institutions develop a more comprehensive risk assessment.
  6. Improve analytical transparency and promote common standards. Enhancing the governance mechanisms, classification systems, and explainability of blockchain analytics tools can improve the transparency and comparability of analytical results while preserving room for technological innovation.
  7. Strengthen inter-institutional cooperation to bridge information gaps. Encourage communication and collaboration among banks, CASPs, public authorities, and other relevant institutions. Within the limits permitted by law, integrate information on on-chain activity, fiat fund flows, and customer backgrounds.
  8. Establish feedback mechanisms to continuously improve reporting quality. Through typology research, thematic guidance, regular quality feedback, and structured dialogue, help reporting institutions understand which information is genuinely valuable and gradually reduce defensive reporting practices.

VII. MistTrack: Helping Turn On-Chain Signals into Verifiable Investigative Leads

For financial institutions, payment institutions, and cryptoasset service providers, what they really need is not simply to identify that an address poses a risk, but to further understand where the risk originates, through which paths it propagates, and how the relevant activity is connected to current transactions.

In this process, MistTrack can serve as a supporting system within on-chain risk identification and investigation workflows, helping teams identify, trace, and organize relevant information.

Building on eight years of experience in blockchain security and threat intelligence, MistTrack has served more than 500 institutional clients, including cryptocurrency exchanges, crypto funds, DeFi platforms, cross-chain bridges, and cross-border payment platforms. It has also received the Gold Award in the FinTech (RegTech: Regulatory and Risk Management) category at the Hong Kong ICT Awards (HKICT Awards).

If you are exploring how to apply on-chain risk identification capabilities to your business scenarios, feel free to contact us for further information.

SlowMist Invited to HKMA Regtech Event to Showcase On-Chain Compliance and Risk Management Capabilities

On November 17, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) hosted an event titled “The Digital Assets Frontier: Deploying Regtech to Mitigate ML/TF Risks” at Two International Finance Centre. The event brought together various banks and financial institutions to discuss how Regtech can be used to address money laundering and terrorist financing risks within the distributed ledger technology (DLT) ecosystem.

As a globally leading blockchain security company, SlowMist was invited to exhibit at the event. At its booth, SlowMist introduced and demonstrated its anti-money laundering (AML) products and solutions to representatives from financial institutions.

On-Site Engagement: Showcasing On-Chain Compliance Practices

The event featured two panel discussions, covering security, industry risks and innovation within the distributed ledger technology (DLT) ecosystem, as well as regulatory oversight and global collaboration. Networking sessions and booth demonstrations were held between the two discussions, providing participating institutions with opportunities to learn about the technologies and services offered by different exhibitors.

During the networking sessions, representatives from several financial institutions visited the SlowMist booth to learn about the practical applications of on-chain compliance tools. Tony, Head of the SlowMist Hong Kong Community, introduced MistTrack and SlowMist KYT, two of SlowMist’s products, through live demonstrations, explaining their features and use cases.

MistTrack is a cryptocurrency compliance and tracing platform serving users worldwide. It provides address label lookups, fund risk analysis, address profiling, behavioral analysis, fund flow tracing and visualization, as well as KYT/KYA APIs. These capabilities help users identify address risks, analyze fund connections, and trace the movement of funds. Currently, MistTrack’s analytical capabilities cover 19 major blockchains, over 100 types of tokens, and 18 stablecoins. It has accumulated more than 500 million entity address labels, covering over 10,000 entities, and integrates sanctions lists and relevant intelligence from the U.S. Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), the UK HM Treasury (UK HMT), and other sources, supporting on-chain risk identification and fund analysis.

For exchanges, banks, funds, and other digital asset service providers, day-to-day compliance management requires not only risk screening of individual addresses but also continuous monitoring and risk identification of transaction activities. SlowMist KYT is a real-time, configurable AML engine designed for institutional compliance teams and virtual asset service providers (VASPs). It supports real-time transaction risk identification, risk exposure path analysis, risk rule configuration, continuous monitoring, alerts and case management, as well as audit trails and risk tracing. These capabilities help institutions integrate on-chain risk monitoring into their existing business processes.

Commenting on the event, Tony, Head of the SlowMist Hong Kong Community, said:

“Many financial institutions are currently exploring virtual asset businesses. However, identifying the identities behind on-chain addresses and navigating the complexity of fund movements have introduced new requirements for institutional compliance and risk management. We are pleased to have this opportunity, provided by the HKMA, to engage face-to-face with various financial institutions and better understand their practical business needs. SlowMist hopes to leverage the on-chain intelligence, address analysis, and fund tracing capabilities accumulated through MistTrack to support institutions in conducting on-chain risk screening and transaction monitoring.”

Looking ahead, SlowMist will continue to address the needs of financial institutions and digital asset service providers in on-chain risk identification, transaction monitoring, and fund tracing by providing blockchain security, AML, and KYT-related products and services, supporting the secure and compliant operation of digital asset businesses.

Analysis | FATF Releases Report on Combating End-to-End Illicit Financial Flows Linked to Scam Compounds

On November 5, 2026, the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) released a report titled Combating End-to-End Illicit Financial Flows Linked to Scam Compounds, analyzing how scam compounds operate and how criminal proceeds are generated, transferred, laundered, and reinvested in further criminal activities. FATF describes scam compounds as one of the faster-growing forms of organized crime globally and estimates that they cause losses amounting to tens of billions of dollars annually. The accompanying document, FATF Principles for Combating Illicit Financial Flows Linked to Scam Compounds, summarizes the response in six principles.

The report points out that scam compounds are evolving from large physical sites into decentralized and mobile networks, often connected to fraud, human trafficking and forced criminality, money laundering, corruption, and various professional services. The accompanying principles document cites an estimate that global fraud causes approximately $500 billion in losses annually. This is an estimate for fraud in general, not losses caused by scam compounds alone.

The following content is based entirely on the report released by FATF. SlowMist has only translated and interpreted the report to help readers quickly understand the information. It does not represent any position taken by SlowMist on the report’s content, views, or conclusions.

Original report: https://www.fatf-gafi.org/en/news/combating-illicit-financial-flows-linked-to-scam-compounds.html

Scam Compounds Are More Like Operational Nodes Within a Network

To understand this report, it is important to first grasp one key point: scam compounds should not be viewed simply as “places where fraud takes place.” They are more like operational nodes within a criminal network. Some individuals are responsible for recruiting and controlling personnel, others build fraud platforms and contact victims, while others handle payment collection and money laundering. Still others provide professional services such as accounts, communications, and virtual asset exchanges. These functions may be handled by a single criminal group or distributed among different organizations and service providers.

This division of labor makes the network harder to identify and easier to relocate when targeted by law enforcement. Large compounds may be broken up into smaller teams operating out of apartments, offices, or short-term rental properties. Recruitment, fraud, payment collection, and money laundering may also take place across different countries. The report therefore recommends looking beyond physical locations and individual transactions to investigate common controllers, shared infrastructure, and key service providers.

Operating Models, Supporting Infrastructure, and Fund Flows

Organizations Can Be Centralized or Decentralized

Scam networks first need to invest in setting up premises and communication infrastructure, recruiting personnel, and purchasing data or advertising. They then collect payments through investment scams, impersonation scams, and other methods. Victims’ money may initially enter personal or corporate accounts, or be transferred through mule accounts, e-wallets, virtual assets, underground banks, or gambling platforms. It may then be withdrawn, exchanged, or used to purchase real estate, vehicles, and luxury goods. Some proceeds go to the controllers, while others are reinvested in recruitment, equipment, premises, and the next round of scams.

The primary source of income is usually investment fraud, including relationship-based scams that first establish trust and then gradually persuade victims to invest more, as well as investment platforms that fabricate trading dashboards, display fake returns, and prevent withdrawals. Other related sources of income may include recruitment fees, the resale of trafficked persons, wage withholding, ransom or release fees, refund recovery scams, online gambling, and other illicit services. Criminal networks may also sell stolen data, fraud tools, underground banking, or money laundering services.

Operating costs themselves can also provide upstream investigative leads. Examples include discrepancies between payroll expenses and the number of personnel, bulk purchases of prepaid SIM cards, domain hosting and cloud computing expenses, land and buildings, recruitment and transportation, security, bribes, and payments to account providers and money laundering service providers. As operations become more decentralized, large bills associated with centralized premises may decrease, replaced by smaller expenses incurred across different locations and service providers.

FATF describes this chain in seven stages: establishing operational conditions, recruiting personnel and identifying victims, carrying out scams, collecting payments, layering and transferring funds, cashing out and integration, and generating profits and reinvesting them. This is an analytical framework, not a fixed process that every case follows. Funds may also skip certain stages or move repeatedly between different stages.

The report notes that cash remains one of the most common channels for moving funds in questionnaires across different jurisdictions. Informal remittance channels and underground banks are also important. Meanwhile, banks and payment institutions, e-wallets, virtual asset service providers, P2P transactions, and stablecoins may all be exploited. The report does not describe virtual assets as the only or necessarily primary channel. Investigations should take local circumstances into account to determine where the money actually comes from and which accounts and services it passes through.

In addition, the report identifies large language models, chatbots, voice cloning, deepfakes, and automated scripts as factors that amplify the scale and adaptability of scams. These technologies can reduce the marginal costs of content localization, translation, and variant testing, while supporting targeted victim selection, identity generation, back-end management, and adjustments to scam scripts. It also points out that automation may change labor requirements. Some operations may rely less on large numbers of coerced workers in the future and more on stable electricity, network connectivity, computing power, and digital infrastructure. Regarding the risks of “agentic AI” autonomously planning and executing multi-step tasks, the report uses forward-looking language, recommending continued monitoring while also paying attention to potential new vulnerabilities arising from manipulation through malicious content, fake websites, or toolchains.

What These Networks Depend On and Where They May Operate

Scam compound activities do not take place in just one type of fixed environment. In the report’s questionnaire, border corridors and logistics routes used to move people, cash, and supplies were the most frequently mentioned factors, followed by insufficient government control or oversight and corruption. Special Economic Zones (SEZs) and Free Trade Zones (FTZs) were mentioned relatively less frequently. The report specifically cautions that these factors must be assessed in their specific contexts: an SEZ does not inherently mean weak regulation, and ordinary urban residences, hotels, and offices may also be used to conduct scams.

Casinos, online gambling, hotels, and related facilities may simultaneously provide operational premises, commercial cover, or fund transfer functions. Nominees, shell and front companies, nominal employers, and professional intermediaries may conceal actual control relationships. Corruption or protection networks may also help criminal groups obtain premises, permits, and security, or gain advance knowledge of law enforcement operations. The report does not treat these characteristics as a profile that every compound will necessarily exhibit. Instead, it recommends verifying them individually in conjunction with control relationships, fund flows, and operating expenses.

In terms of financial channels, cash remains one of the most commonly observed forms across jurisdictions in the questionnaires. Informal remittance/value transfer services (MVTS) and underground banks are also important. In addition, banks and payment institutions, e-wallets, virtual asset service providers (VASPs), peer-to-peer (P2P) transactions, over-the-counter (OTC) channels, and stablecoins may all be involved in collecting, exchanging, or transferring funds. Mule accounts (accounts used to receive and transfer scam proceeds, whose holders may be aware of their involvement or may be deceived or coerced), corporate accounts, virtual account numbers, cross-chain services, and gambling platforms may also be exploited. The report does not describe virtual assets as the only or always the primary form of fund movement. Specific investigations still need to examine how funds actually enter and leave in the local context.

Beyond financial channels, scam networks also rely on social media, communication services, SIM cards and SIM boxes (devices that can hold large numbers of SIM cards and make bulk calls or send bulk text messages), domains and hosting, cloud computing, VPNs, online advertising, fake websites and applications, data brokers, and customer management tools. Legitimate technologies and services are not inherently the source of risk. The key question is whether they are being abused by specific criminal networks. The report provides an illustrative classification of 54 dependencies and identifies 14 potential critical dependencies. Whether a particular facility is critical depends on whether it is shared by multiple units, whether alternatives are available, and how long the network would need to recover if it were disrupted.

Following the Money: How the Seven Stages Connect

The operational and support networks discussed above ultimately all come down to money. The report views scam compounds as criminal enterprises that continuously generate, transfer, launder, and reinvest funds, and uses seven stages to help readers understand this chain:

Stage 1: Establishing operational premises and supporting infrastructure: Investments in premises, buildings, communications and IT, recruitment, transportation, documents, security, bribes, front companies, and financial/money laundering channels.

Stage 2: Acquiring labor and victims: Fake job recruitment, cross-border transportation, accommodation or visa arrangements, and forced criminality take place alongside the identification of online victims through social media, dating apps, fake investment platforms, or online gambling channels.

Stage 3: Carrying out scams and extracting proceeds: Investment scams, impersonation scams, phishing, business email compromise (BEC), gambling-related scams, ransom, refund recovery scams, and others. Victims may face repeated demands to “recharge, pay taxes, unlock funds, or withdraw,” or be induced to authorize token transfers from their wallets.

Stage 4: Collecting funds and initial placement: Funds enter personal, corporate, or mule-controlled bank accounts, e-wallets, or virtual asset wallets. Victims may also hand over cash, precious metals, or gift cards, or be directed to purchase high-value goods as a means of monetization. The report cites cases in which funds were transferred within just two minutes.

Stage 5: Layering and concealment: Funds are moved through mule networks, corporate accounts, e-wallets, P2P virtual asset transactions, unlicensed MVTS, OTC channels, offshore VASPs, underground banks, cross-chain bridges, mixing services, cross-chain conversions, cryptocurrency ATMs, or gambling platforms. Underground banks can deliver equivalent amounts through counterpart payments in different jurisdictions, reducing the need for direct cross-border transfers.

Stage 6: Cashing out and integration: Funds are withdrawn in cash, virtual assets are converted back into fiat currency, or funds are transferred through services such as hawala (an informal remittance system originating in South Asia and the Middle East, in which a customer in one location gives money to an intermediary, while a corresponding intermediary in another location delivers an equivalent amount based on a verbal instruction or code. The two parties settle their accounts afterward, and the funds often do not physically cross borders, leaving fewer banking records; this is a general explanation, not wording from the original report). Funds may also be stored in vaults or invested in real estate, luxury goods, vehicles, precious metals, front companies (businesses that appear to operate legitimate activities but actually serve as cover), and other assets.

Stage 7: Profit extraction, reinvestment, and expansion: Controllers take their profits while using part of the proceeds for salaries, guards, recruitment, transportation, corruption, premises, digital infrastructure, and new scam operations.

The seven stages are an analytical framework, not a fixed process that every case will follow from beginning to end. Networks may enter at any stage and may repeatedly cycle through different stages. External service providers may also support multiple stages simultaneously. The report cites examples in which funds are transferred within minutes, while in other cases, underground banks deliver equivalent amounts across different jurisdictions to avoid direct cross-border transfers. Fund flow mapping needs to be examined alongside upstream operating expenses, recruitment networks, shared accounts, and final assets.

Challenges in Disruption and Response Principles

Why Disruption Is Always One Step Behind

Victims often authorize payments themselves under manipulation, so the payments may not necessarily appear suspicious. The payment institution may only see an ordinary transfer, while the receiving institution may see funds being rapidly consolidated or withdrawn without understanding how the victim was deceived. The report uses Thailand’s experience to illustrate this time gap: funds may leave the financial system within 3 to 5 minutes, while victims take an average of approximately 20 hours to realize they have been scammed. Suspicious transaction reports are useful for subsequent financial intelligence and investigations, but they generally cannot serve as a real-time payment blocking mechanism on their own.

Disruption efforts are also affected by fragmented information, cross-border authority, and evidentiary requirements. Platforms, telecommunications companies, banks, law enforcement agencies, and victim support organizations each have access to only part of the picture. Even when leads are shared, their sources must be verified, additional context must be provided, and the information must reach entities capable of taking action. Cases involving multiple jurisdictions also involve mutual legal assistance, overseas data preservation, virtual asset tracing, corporate beneficial ownership, and victim screening. Freezing accounts is only an intermediate step; subsequent confiscation, recovery, and return of funds depend on different legal procedures.

Underreporting further exacerbates these problems. The report cites an estimate from the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC) that approximately 70% of fraud victims do not report the incidents. This figure relates to fraud victims more broadly, not specifically to scam compounds. Online victims may refrain from seeking help due to shame, fear, or the belief that their losses cannot be recovered. People who have been trafficked or forced to carry out scams may worry about being treated as criminals, facing retaliation, or experiencing immigration-related consequences.

Response Approach: From the Source to Fund Recovery

When discussing response measures, the report divides actions into upstream and downstream efforts. Upstream efforts focus on identifying and disrupting the conditions that scam compounds rely on to establish, maintain, and expand their operations, such as recruitment, advertising, telecommunications, domains, hosting, fake platforms, premises, and professional services. Downstream efforts focus on victim payments and scam proceeds, including intercepting or recalling payments, tracing mule accounts and wallets, preserving assets, and advancing freezing, confiscation, recovery, and return of funds. The so-called “payment window” refers to the brief period after money has been sent but before it can be transferred or cashed out. Investigations themselves can cover both upstream and downstream activities simultaneously. Therefore, the report proposes a combined approach rather than claiming that any single institutional model or technical solution has been proven optimal.

Principle 1: The scope of disruption should cover the broader criminal network.

Investigations should extend to controllers, recruiters, money laundering service providers, and the accounts, platforms, and communication infrastructure shared by multiple scam units. Dealing only with the physical premises or low-level operatives may not be enough to deprive the network of its operational capabilities.

Principle 2: Trace the entire chain from recruitment and victim targeting to asset recovery.

Actions should not wait until funds enter banking or virtual asset channels. Recruitment, advertising, and victim engagement may also leave early warning signs. After funds are collected, they should be traced as quickly as possible, assets should be preserved, and confiscation and return of funds should be pursued in accordance with the law.

Principle 3: Connect financial, technological, and telecommunications intelligence.

Banks, payment institutions, platforms, and telecommunications service providers each hold part of the available intelligence. The principles document advocates cross-sector cooperation to turn this information into actionable intelligence under lawful authority, privacy safeguards, and clear response procedures.

Principle 4: Cross-border action must take place before funds become uncontrollable.

Funds may move across accounts, assets, and jurisdictions within just a few minutes. Relevant parties need to establish points of contact and rapid response channels in advance, ensuring that leads are delivered as early as possible to institutions capable of blocking payments or preserving funds. Subsequent investigations and judicial procedures must still be completed in accordance with applicable laws.

Principle 5: Make victim protection an integral part of the response.

Accessible reporting channels should be provided, trafficked and coerced individuals should be identified and protected, and safeguards against penalization should be established. Protection should not be conditional on victims providing intelligence or cooperating with investigations.

Principle 6: Evaluate long-term effectiveness and remain alert to criminal displacement.

A single raid, website shutdown, or account freeze may cause criminal activities to move to new locations, platforms, or service providers. Evaluations should focus on whether fraud losses have decreased, funds have become more difficult to transfer, and critical service capabilities have been sustainably disrupted, rather than merely counting arrests or shutdowns.

Turning Cooperation Mechanisms into Concrete Action

The report summarizes six types of cooperation arrangements: domestic anti-fraud centers, multi-agency task forces or joint action teams, shared fraud data platforms, rapid response and asset preservation networks, cross-border financial intelligence and law enforcement networks, and “networks of networks” that connect existing platforms. These arrangements do not require every jurisdiction to adopt the same model. The key is to clarify in advance who holds what information, who can take what action, how information can be lawfully transferred, and what the response timelines and escalation conditions are.

The report cites examples including India’s I4C, Australia’s FIRESTORM, Indonesia’s IASC, Malaysia’s NSRC, Singapore’s FRONTIER+, and the Anti-Deception Coordination Centre (ADCC) in Hong Kong, China. Cross-border mechanisms also include INTERPOL operations, Europol’s Rapid Response Protocol pilot, and rapid response channels within the Egmont Network. INTERPOL Silver Notices can help identify, trace, and monitor criminal assets abroad, but do not themselves provide a legal basis for freezing or confiscation. Subsequent measures must still be based on domestic law or formal cooperation mechanisms.

What Can Be Done in Practice

Risk assessments and network mapping can first identify a jurisdiction’s position within the network: it may be the location of a scam compound, the source of victims, a recruitment or transit location, a money laundering hub, a place where assets are held, or a host of critical digital infrastructure. Combining financial transactions with advertising, recruitment, telecommunications, and digital leads can help identify common controllers, shared accounts, operating expenses, beneficial ownership, and professional intermediaries. Fraud classifications should also record payment methods, whether victims authorized payments under manipulation, network connections, and fund recovery status, making it easier for different institutions to identify the same fraudulent activities.

Shared data mechanisms need to clearly define their legal basis, purpose of use, participants, common data fields, data sources and quality, retention periods, correction and review procedures, and security controls. Examples such as France’s IBAN Fraud Register, South Korea’s ASAP platform, and the UK’s Scam Signals demonstrate different approaches to sharing risk signals across institutions. Where information may lead to adverse consequences such as account restrictions, accuracy requirements and review channels should be established. The effectiveness data published by some platforms is also not specific to scam compounds alone.

Rapid response mechanisms can establish 24/7 points of contact, request templates, escalation standards, and response timelines, allowing leads to reach financial institutions, VASPs, or stablecoin issuers capable of controlling payments, accounts, or wallets as quickly as possible. The report particularly emphasizes the initial 24 to 72 hours after discovery or reporting as crucial for tracing, recovering, and returning funds. Measures may include alerts, suspensions, payment blocking, recalls, account or wallet restrictions, and temporary asset preservation. Subsequent freezing and confiscation must still be handled in accordance with the law.

Upstream disruption can target identified scam advertisements, malicious domains, fake websites or applications, bulk SIM facilities, hosting, and back-end infrastructure. When taking down or blocking these resources, evidence such as devices, domains, advertising payments, and contact channels should be preserved as much as possible, while also monitoring whether criminal activities move to successor infrastructure. Investigations into mule accounts should distinguish between knowing participants and individuals who have been deceived or coerced. Relationships can be identified by examining devices, locations, transfer times, withdrawal patterns, and multi-layer account chains, while avoiding unnecessary financial exclusion.

Corporate and beneficial ownership analysis can trace nominees, shell or front companies, common directors and addresses, cross-border ownership chains, and successor entities. Electronic evidence must be preserved promptly, with the chain of custody maintained. Virtual asset tracing should also avoid relying solely on on-chain labels. Wallet ownership and address clustering should be based on verifiable methodologies and cross-checked against VASP customer information, fiat on- and off-ramps, device communications, and corporate records.

Case Studies: What Measures Have Been Implemented and Where Their Limitations Lie

The report’s annex brings together investigation and cooperation cases from different jurisdictions. Coordinated actions by the United States and the United Kingdom against organizations such as Prince Group combined sanctions, asset seizures (the report states that more than $15 billion in assets were seized), and investigations into companies and leadership. Meanwhile, Hong Kong police and law enforcement agencies in Taiwan, China, separately took action against shared infrastructure providing telecommunications services to scam compounds. These cases demonstrate an approach that investigates further upstream into the network by tracing shared services and control relationships.

During a “Disruption Week” operation, the United States’ interagency Scam Center Strike Force disrupted approximately 1.4 million social media and email accounts, as well as malicious network infrastructure. The operation supported arrests in Thailand and led to the voluntary freezing of more than $3.8 million in virtual assets. Indonesia’s Anti-Scam Centre (IASC) blocked more than 700,000 accounts between November 2024 and September 2026 and returned approximately $11.55 million to victims. The UK’s Scam Signals uses mobile network risk signals to help banks identify risks. Citing the Global System for Mobile Communications Association (GSMA), the report states that banks’ use of such signals was associated with a 41% reduction in the number of people deceived and a 44% decrease in fraud losses. However, “associated with” does not independently establish a causal relationship.

Other cases also illustrate the limitations of these actions. Italy used suspicious transaction reports, corporate information, and open-source intelligence to map cross-border fund networks, but their connection to any specific physical scam compound has not yet been confirmed. In Brazil, a stablecoin issuer assisted in temporarily freezing assets held in self-custody wallets, but freezing does not mean confiscation, recovery, or return of funds. Cases in Cambodia, Thailand, and India involved screening, interviewing, and protecting repatriated individuals. Given the differences in legal frameworks and data definitions across jurisdictions, these materials illustrate possible approaches rather than directly comparable rankings of effectiveness.

FATF believes that the evidence supporting downstream measures, such as blocking payments and tracing proceeds, is relatively strong. Whether upstream disruption targeting advertisements, recruitment, malicious domains, and phone numbers can sustainably weaken criminal capabilities still requires more practical experience and evaluation.

Conclusion

The FATF report presents a networked, cross-border, and cyclical model of criminal operations. Scam compounds are not necessarily confined to large physical compounds. Recruitment, victim acquisition, scam execution, payment collection, money laundering, and technical support can be distributed across different locations and handled by different criminal groups or professional service providers. Criminal proceeds are cashed out and concealed before flowing back into premises, personnel, and the next round of scams, in turn supporting the network’s expansion.

This means that risks are difficult to fully understand by examining a single transaction or one type of asset alone. Victims may authorize payments themselves under manipulation, while relevant leads are scattered across banks, payment institutions, VASPs, platforms, telecommunications companies, and law enforcement agencies. Cash, informal remittances, and underground banks remain important, while virtual assets are just one of several channels. Therefore, the report emphasizes connecting network investigations, financial intelligence, rapid payment intervention, cross-border cooperation, and asset recovery, while incorporating victim protection into the response process. Individuals who have been trafficked or forced to participate in scams should be identified as victims through screening rather than simply treated as voluntary criminals.

At the on-chain level, the report also emphasizes the need for verifiable methodologies. Virtual asset tracing should not rely solely on labels to draw conclusions, but should be cross-checked against VASP customer information, fiat on- and off-ramps, device communications, and corporate records. On-chain anti-money laundering tools such as SlowMist KYT and MistTrack can provide capabilities including address labeling, risk scoring, fund tracing, and transaction monitoring. These tools can help VASPs, stablecoin-related institutions, and other organizations identify whether funds are associated with high-risk sources, visualize fund flows, and provide leads for suspicious transaction analysis and reporting.

Effectiveness also needs to be evaluated over the long term: Have victim losses decreased? Have assets actually been recovered and returned? Have key accounts, services, and infrastructure been continuously disrupted? Or has the network simply moved to a different location or channel? FATF also points out that the existing evidence of effectiveness is uneven. In particular, whether upstream disruption can sustainably weaken criminal capabilities still requires more practical experience and evaluation. Jurisdictions should select measures based on their local risks, legal authority, and available resources, and continuously assess the actual results.

item.title: U.S. OFAC Sanctions Individuals and Entities Linked to DPRK IT Worker Networks
item.dc:creator: SlowMist
item.content:encoded:
Recently, the U.S. Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the designation of 10 individuals and one entity. According to the U.S. Department of the Treasury, these targets were involved in facilitating overseas IT worker networks operated by the North Korean government. Individuals involved used false identities and documents to gain employment at companies in the United States and other countries, and transferred their earnings to the North Korean government. The action also targets individuals accused of facilitating fund conversions, cryptocurrency transfers, and team operations.

Sanctions Action

The targets of OFAC’s action include IT workers, team leaders, financial intermediaries, and related entities operating in North Korea and Russia.

The announcement disclosed several cryptocurrency-related activities:

  • Russian national Vitold Viktorovich Obertas was accused of conducting nearly $2 million in cryptocurrency conversions and at least $1.25 million in other currency transactions for North Korean officials since January 2025.
  • Kim Ki Hyok was accused of transferring nearly $500,000 worth of cryptocurrency for an IT worker team operating in Russia since 2024.
  • Kim Hyo Dong was accused of providing logistical support to another team and facilitating the transfer of more than $100,000 in financial assets.
  • Russian national Ilya Aleksandrovich Boykov was accused of assisting the related entity with approximately $3.5 million in cryptocurrency exchanges and transfers since 2024.
  • First Financial and Technical Development Center (FFTDC) was accused of deploying North Korean IT workers in Russia. According to the announcement, its personnel have collectively generated more than $750,000 in revenue for the North Korean government since 2025.

Analysis of Sanctioned Address Connections

The SDN List updated by OFAC that day listed eight digital currency addresses associated with the designated parties, spanning the Ethereum and TRON blockchains.

According to analysis by MistTrack, SlowMist’s anti-money laundering and on-chain tracing tool, observable connections exist between these addresses: some transferred funds directly to one another, while multiple addresses transferred funds to the same wallet identified as an exchange deposit address.

Among them, the Ethereum address 0x761edd5e4546229a0bd35ae99b4d3d01cf4a3510 is listed under both Boykov and Obertas, making it a clear point of address overlap in the list.

Kim Ki Hyok

According to OFAC, since 2024, Kim Ki Hyok has transferred nearly $500,000 worth of cryptocurrency for an IT worker team operating in Russia. The Ethereum address associated with him on the list is:

0xE4C9a7F68B1EbA4508f54f07f7378847318dD1A3

This is the “cleanest” and most limited address in the entire list: it existed for only two days and performed just one transaction, transferring 50,000 DAI to an exchange.

The funds first passed through an intermediary address, 0x4865773f498186d838fe47227804a158cbed51de. On August 31, four addresses transferred a total of approximately 100,000 DAI to this intermediary address. On September 9 at 06:46, the intermediary address transferred 50,000 DAI to the address listed under Kim’s name. Approximately six minutes later, it transferred another 0.001 ETH to cover the transaction fee. At 09:39 the following day, the address listed under Kim’s name transferred the 50,000 DAI to Bybit deposit address 0x197c6c66d9fc674d496ee232f418bd6f6013a13b.

Ilya Aleksandrovich Boykov

According to OFAC, since 2024, Russian national Boykov has assisted the related entity with approximately $3.5 million in cryptocurrency exchanges and transfers. The Ethereum addresses associated with him on the list include:

0x12Ea80238C7d805D003ce793594e92d84A6f4E8d

0x761edd5e4546229a0bd35ae99b4d3d01cf4a3510

MistTrack’s analysis of address 0x12Ea8 shows that it was active from November 10, 2022, to August 25, 2025, receiving a total of 49.5767 ETH, 4.7 million USDC, 4.63 million USDT, and 10.22 million DAI.

Its token funds had four clearly identifiable outflows:

  • 50.54% (approximately $9.88 million) was transferred directly to the Bybit deposit address 0x761edd5e4546229a0bd35ae99b4d3d01cf4a3510 associated with BOYKOV/Obertas. The largest single transfer was 511,000 USDC on June 12, 2024. An additional 13.67 ETH was also transferred to this Bybit deposit address.
  • 20.47% (approximately $4 million) was deposited into Bybit deposit address 0x197c6c66d9fc674d496ee232f418bd6f6013a13b across 31 transactions.
  • 28.88% (approximately $5.65 million) was deposited into two HTX deposit addresses: 0xee60121c763143a4fb17735ab86b5f0fc5cb1800 and 0x7f78ddf455f9f8eef56c4c9f76b5d53c75dc54ee. The first transfer occurred on June 22, 2023, and transfers continued without interruption for more than two years thereafter.
  • 0.05% ($9,870) was deposited into Binance deposit address 0x4941c9481e9bb27b74be4e2b6c6fa349f8be99d5.

Shared Address of Boykov and Obertas

0x761edd5e4546229a0bd35ae99b4d3d01cf4a3510

MistTrack has labeled this address as a Bybit deposit address, and OFAC officially lists it under both Obertas and Boykov.

In terms of fund composition, 128 transactions from Boykov’s address 0x12Ea80238C7d805D003ce793594e92d84A6f4E8d accounted for 77% of its total inflows. These transactions spanned from June 22, 2023, to July 25, 2025. Tracing this address further upstream also revealed connections to addresses labeled as DPRK by MistTrack.

Two additional TRON addresses are listed under Boykov: TQKoDq5aCrWAciiNtete5pDYVN38i4qFN1 and TXmrnVgsqCMJncYHTXchuJ5z111BXSj4g3.

Address TQKoDq5aCrWAciiNtete5pDYVN38i4qFN1 is Boykov’s first wallet on TRON. Its transaction volume is relatively small, but the flow of funds is clear. From December 2, 2022, to December 21, 2025, it received a total of 873,675 USDT. Its largest outgoing transfer was 257,732 USDT, sent directly to Obertas’s Bybit deposit address TFksjBcHPYqgAax2USheQuaT1ydRKyZRdg, while the remaining funds were distributed across various destinations.

Address TXmrnVgsqCMJncYHTXchuJ5z111BXSj4g3 is Boykov’s more concentrated and later-activated wallet on TRON, and also the most direct connection point between him and Obertas. From March 21, 2024, to December 6, 2025, it received a total of 1.62 million USDT. Within three months, it transferred 1.4 million USDT (86.2%) in seven transactions, all to Obertas’s Bybit deposit address TFksjBcHPYqgAax2USheQuaT1ydRKyZRdg. Its fund sources were primarily medium-sized clients.

The direct transfers between these two TRON addresses and TFksjBcHPYqgAax2USheQuaT1ydRKyZRdg provide on-chain evidence linking addresses listed under Boykov to those listed under Obertas.

In addition to the Ethereum address jointly listed under Boykov and Obertas, OFAC also lists three TRON addresses under Obertas:

TCV4qdpTxoMyqkn7sSPeRrXmhH5JFxMvmT

TQCBdU4K92oxLAkzwexZpqVZJhmPbtLYMm

TFksjBcHPYqgAax2USheQuaT1ydRKyZRdg

Address TCV4qdpTxoMyqkn7sSPeRrXmhH5JFxMvmT has been labeled by MistTrack as an HTX deposit address. Over the 11-month period from September 10, 2024, to August 28, 2025, it received a total of 9.16 million USDT.

Address TQCBdU4K92oxLAkzwexZpqVZJhmPbtLYMm is an address with multiple incoming and outgoing transactions. Analysis shows that it received approximately 11.09 million USDT between November 7, 2022, and February 25, 2026, and transferred funds to other addresses. Of this amount, approximately 2.58 million USDT was transferred to Obertas’s own Bybit deposit address TFksjBcHPYqgAax2USheQuaT1ydRKyZRdg, while approximately 1.08 million USDT was transferred to Obertas’s own HTX deposit address TCV4qdpTxoMyqkn7sSPeRrXmhH5JFxMvmT. These two transfers link TQCBdU4K92oxLAkzwexZpqVZJhmPbtLYMm to the other two addresses listed under Obertas in the sanctions list.

The largest incoming transfer originated from TEvYL8PU8EiC84kAoN67ZhHyUgPfvgVoD8, amounting to 1,242,541 USDT. The transaction activity of this address is relatively complex.

Address TFksjBcHPYqgAax2USheQuaT1ydRKyZRdg has been labeled by MistTrack as a Bybit deposit address. Between March 7, 2023, and October 31, 2026, it received a cumulative total of approximately 31.02 million USDT.

Its second-largest source of funds was Obertas’s own wallet address TQCBdU4K92oxLAkzwexZpqVZJhmPbtLYMm (2.58 million USDT), while its sixth-largest source was Boykov’s address TXmrnVgsqCMJncYHTXchuJ5z111BXSj4g3 (1.4 million USDT).

Taken together, records from both Ethereum and TRON reveal several types of address relationships that can be confirmed or observed:

  • The Ethereum address 0x761ed is listed under both Boykov and Obertas. Boykov’s address 0x12Ea8 previously transferred approximately $9.88 million to it.
  • The Ethereum addresses listed under Boykov and Kim have both transferred funds to 0x197c6. This address is not among the eight addresses published by OFAC in this action.
  • Both TRON addresses listed under Boykov have transferred USDT to the Bybit deposit address TFksj listed under Obertas.
  • Obertas’s address TQCBd has transferred USDT to his own Bybit deposit address TFksj and HTX deposit address TCV4q.

How DPRK IT Worker Networks Operate

These schemes often begin with what appears to be an entirely ordinary remote job: a company posts a vacancy, receives resumes, conducts interviews, then ships a computer and pays a monthly salary. The risk is that the person sitting on the other side of the screen may not be the person named on the resume.

Some DPRK IT workers use stolen, borrowed, or forged identity documents to apply for remote positions. They also prepare corresponding email accounts, social media accounts, and professional work histories. Some use VPNs, proxy networks, or facilitators located in target countries to conceal their actual locations. Computers shipped by companies may first be delivered to local individuals or “laptop farms” and then operated remotely by overseas personnel. As a result, the addresses, identity information, and device locations seen by companies may not reflect where the actual workers are located.

These arrangements typically require coordination among multiple people. Some provide or rent out identities, others receive and store devices, assist with opening payment accounts, or manage teams and transfer earnings. Facilitators may know whom they are helping, or they may simply believe they are providing ordinary receiving, networking, or outsourcing services.

Income is typically generated in the form of salaries from remote work or project payments. Funds may be transferred through third-party bank accounts, payment platforms, and cryptocurrency addresses. Some of the individuals named in this OFAC action were specifically accused of facilitating cryptocurrency conversions, fund transfers, or team operations. For companies, however, the issue goes beyond whether an employee’s identity is genuine. Once remote workers gain access to corporate accounts and devices, they may be able to access code repositories, customer information, internal tools, and other systems. In some cases, after being discovered, these individuals have used previously obtained access privileges to steal corporate data and demand payments by threatening to publicly disclose or withhold the data.

Therefore, a more practical approach for companies is to assess identity verification, device delivery, contractor management, and system permissions together: verify who is doing the work and what they can access.

Conclusion

The risks posed by DPRK IT workers can extend from the recruitment process to devices and system permissions. When verifying candidates, companies should check not only their identities and work histories, but also whether their locations, device delivery addresses, and payment accounts are consistent with one another. For remote employees, outsourced personnel, and third-party service providers, companies should continuously verify who actually uses the devices and which systems their accounts can access, while avoiding granting permissions beyond what their work requires.

For cryptocurrency exchanges, custodians, payment service providers, and other relevant institutions, the individuals, entities, and wallet addresses on the OFAC list should also be incorporated into routine screening. On November 2, during Hong Kong FinTech Week, the “Legal Breakthrough, Risk Foundation | 2026 HK Institutional RWA & Stablecoin Forum,” co-hosted by SlowMist and JunHe LLP, was held at AIA Central in Central, Hong Kong.

The event brought together institutional representatives and industry guests from securities firms, financial institutions, payment technology, blockchain security, and legal services. Discussions focused on RWA issuance and circulation, stablecoin payments, institutional compliance, and on-chain security. Participants exchanged insights from the perspectives of business practices, legal compliance, and technical security, exploring practical approaches to implementing digital asset-related businesses and managing associated risks.

At the beginning of the event, Keywolf, Partner & CPO of SlowMist, delivered the opening keynote, titled “In the AI Era, Everyone Can Find Vulnerabilities: How Should Institutions Strengthen Security Protection and Anti-Money Laundering Screening?” He pointed out that AI technology has lowered the barriers to launching attacks and causing damage, making it increasingly important for institutions to understand how attackers’ methods are evolving. In terms of security protection, rather than focusing solely on sudden “black swan” events, institutions should pay greater attention to “gray rhino” risks that persist over time but are easily overlooked. Meanwhile, institutions need to establish a zero-trust mechanism covering personnel, systems, and code, and enhance their security capabilities through continuous verification, combined with AI technology and mature industry tools.

Regarding anti-money laundering screening, Keywolf analyzed the current compliance costs faced by institutions from the perspectives of technical tools, personnel, and legal services. He pointed out that when selecting compliance tools, institutions need to comprehensively consider their budgets, business scale, and actual management needs. Subsequently, Jacqueline Qiao, Partner at JunHe LLP, delivered a presentation on “Hong Kong Virtual Asset and Stablecoin Payment-Related License Applications and Key Compliance Considerations.” She provided a detailed introduction to the legal and regulatory matters that institutions need to consider when planning their businesses in these areas, offering compliance-related references for institutions interested in entering the Hong Kong market.

The two keynote presentations addressed technical security and legal compliance from different perspectives, also laying the groundwork for the three subsequent roundtable discussions.

The first roundtable, themed “Ecosystem Support, Fund Operations, and Licensed Investment Banks and Securities Firms: How Can Traditional Assets Truly Become Tradable On-Chain Products?”, was moderated by Alma Li, Founder & CEO of Techub News, and featured Bobo Lee, Manager of Blockchain and Digital Asset, Cyberport; Yuky Yu, Global Lead Digital Asset Service Delivery, Bolder Group; Thomas Tam, Managing Director Investment Banking, Eddid Financial; and Terence Wu, Vice President Asset Management Department, CMB International.

Subsequently, the discussion expanded from the tokenization of traditional assets to the business expansion of payments and financial services. The discussion featured Andy Liu, Co-Founder, Tevau; Elaine Huang, Director, CPLUS Securities Limited; and Neo Shen, Senior Sales Manager, PhotonPay.

As customer needs for cross-border fund transfers and financial services continue to evolve, how payment institutions and FinTech companies can move beyond single business models became the focus of this discussion. The guests shared their approaches to expanding business boundaries in areas such as cross-border payments and receipts, stablecoins and payment products, and securities services. They further discussed operational challenges arising from different currencies, time zones, and clearing rules. The discussion also extended from basic payment tools to comprehensive financial services, exploring how product design and operational mechanisms can reduce coordination costs between different business segments to better meet customers’ diverse needs for efficiency, service, and security.

The third roundtable was themed “When On-Chain Transactions Meet AI-Powered Attacks and Defense: How Can Institutions Respond to Security Black Swan Events and Safeguard the Last Line of Defense for On-Chain Funds?” It was moderated by Wendy, BD Manager at ME Group. Keywolf, Partner & CPO of SlowMist; Jacqueline Qiao, Partner at JunHe LLP; Royce Chow, Founder of Ninkr AI; and Adam Dai, Head of Hong Kong, Safeheron, shared their perspectives from the fields of blockchain security, legal services, AI technology, and digital asset custody.

Going forward, SlowMist will continue to focus on blockchain security, leveraging its technical expertise in security audits, threat intelligence, on-chain tracing, and anti-money laundering to strengthen communication and collaboration with industry institutions and ecosystem partners. SlowMist will continue to provide security support for digital asset-related businesses and contribute to the industry’s steady development.
